subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The whole inference,
however, is that which I have stated and which has been conveyed many times by hon. members who are associated with the hon. gentleman. To-morrow we are going to welcome the Prime Minister of New Zealand. Let me say that sitting around the Prime Minister are those who last summer, during the Ontario provincial elections, circulated a pamphlet declaring that the New Zealand government's policies were worse than those of nazi Germany. Yet the spokesman for the government, and the official opposition, will welcome the Prime Minister of New Zealand here to-morrow afternoon. I say that the criticism that is often made of other countries does not take everything into account.
Por example, the rates which are in effect in New Zealand relieve the population there of very heavy obligations. They do not require the same life insurance, they do not require 
the same health insurance, the same medical fees, the same medicine, the same hospitalization, and so on. Those things are met out of what are sometimes referred to as tax levies in this sister nation of the British commonwealth. So I say that when we come to appraise what is happening in another country, let us be fair about it and say what the people of that country are getting for the levies they pay. By comparison, Canada falls well at the foot of the list of nations with social security programmes.
I turn now to the minister's proposal that forced savings be abandoned. Let. me say to him at once that I am glad it has been found possible in the light of our financial position to lower the total levies upon these people. That, of course, is the immediate effect of the proposal, and I am glad it has been found practicable to risk this reduction without danger to our war effort. However, what the government proposes is in effect the taking away of the rose and leaving the-thorn. If it is necessary to collect money from the low income group, why should it not be taken in the form of refundable savings rather than in the form of pure taxes? What we propose is this: let the full amount to be paid by the low income groups at the new rates be paid in as savings to be returned with interest after the war. Pure taxation could start with the higher incomes, and at such a point the proportion of refundable savings could taper off. The rates on the lower incomes proposed by the government can remain in force; the same total revenue would be made available for the war effort, but the burden on the substandard wage and salary earners would be lightened through the return of their payments after the war.
I believe that when I say this I speak for the vast majority of the Canadian people. Statistics of the 1941 census revealed that sixty-two per cent of all-I would draw attention to the word "all"-wage and salary earners made less than $950 a year. If these people must be taxed, let some or all of their taxes be refundable after the war. If exemptions are not to be raised substantially above the present levels of $660 for single persons and $1,200 for married, surely what we propose is the fairest course of all. I think our proposal will be found both equitable and practical. Refundable savings in. the hands of those who will need them most in the post-war years is highly desirable. In the minister's own words, "a reserve of savings will be of great value to the individual and the nation after the war."
Needed purchasing power would thus be put into circulation to assist in maintaining employment. The danger of inflation during

The Budget-Mr. Coldivell
the war would be curtailed, but in addition-
I regard this as most important-deflation would be forestalled after the war. As for war production, it would be stimulated further under this proposal than under that of the government; for added incentive would be given the low income workers through the knowledge that whatever they paid in now would be refundable to them after the war. As for the administrative machinery with regard to these refundable savings, it has been built up and it ought not to be dismantled.
Let me quote in further support of this proposal the survey of the Canadian publishers' war finance publicity committee. A cross-section of the people were asked, "How long could you get along if you lost your job?" The replies reveal that over fifteen per cent could not get along for as much as one month, and many of those expressing no opinion must be added to this group. Another thirteen per cent could not get along for more than two months. If, therefore, collections must be made from the low income groups, let them be made in the form of savings returnable with interest in the after-the-war years. But alternatively I propose, and this proposal is to my mind the most equitable of all, that the exemption on low incomes be raised. Single incomes of say $1,000 or less and married incomes of say $1,500, or $1,600 a year, as has already been moved to-day, could be exempted altogether from either forced savings or taxation. The necessary revenue can then be found in the retention of refundable savings in the higher income brackets and an upward revision of the high income rates; indeed even, as I have suggested before, putting a ceiling on high incomes.
It is strange that at this time, when Great Britain is continuing refundable savings both as an equitable war measure and as a lever for post-war reconstruction, this government should find that the only way to afford taxation relief is to abandon this feature, this device of compulsory savings refundable after the war. In my opinion, as I have already suggested, there are other fairer ways of affording the needed relief.
The tax proposals that I have just put forward are essentially directed toward a democratic realization of fairer income distribution throughout the entire nation. In that direction, Mr. Speaker, we think lies social justice, individual security, and a conception of national unity as yet undreamt of.
The minister boasted in his speech that our public debt is widely held, and I confess that much has been accomplished during the war along these lines. Much too has been accomplished in relieving the nation of foreign obligations, a fact which convinces me that this country is able to stand on its own feet economically if it but has the will to do so. But much remains to be done in the matter of fairer distribution of income.
During the fiscal year 1943-44 some 58 per cent of the victory loans were subscribed by special names and corporations. Furthermore, the government supplemented its borrowings through victory loans by loans from private banks to the extent, in round figures, of $170,000,000, and by the issue of treasury bills. Thus there is already a substantial portion of the public debt in the hands of a few. But what is worse is that the concentration of wealth may be seriously aggravated after the cessation of hostilities as small holders sell their bonds to the banks and to other financial concerns. May I say just here that that is where the refundable nature of the levy might assist us after the war. At one point in his speech the minister says that substantial numbers of bonds will be cashed in by small holders in the immediate post-war period, and at another point he states that the debt will be widely held. Yet it will be the speculators and the big holders who will be taking up the cashed bonds after the war.
The present concentration of wealth in their hands will in my opinion after the war be intensified because our present taxation methods make that almost certain. With this and other factors in mind the party which I have the honour to represent have proposed that the government guarantee victory bonds to the extent of one hundred cents on the dollar for the protection of the small holders against depreciation or speculation. The large holder can indeed hold the victory bonds to the date of maturity, when he will collect one hundred cents on the dollar. Further, we have consistently proposed that the tax structure be adjusted so that the financial burden of the war will fall where it can best be borne, not so much on the little men but more heavily on the war profits and incomes of wealthy individuals and the large corporations.
Further, we propose that the chartered banks be nationalized so that essential war and post-war financing can be accomplished at the smallest cost to the people through the medium of nationally-owned banks controlling currency and credit in terms of the nation's need. Speaking of banks, it is utterly fantastic that the government should pay interest to the banks on money which it has itself created by the issue of government securities. Yet that is what is being done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member a question?

436u
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not interrupt the minister when he was making his speech, and my time is limited. I say that that is what is being done, and bank profits, and, of course, the notorious inner reserves, largely stem from this financial sleight of hand. This is not a trifling matter at a time when the banks hold, according to the member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght), and I did not hear his statement contradicted, some $2,500 million in government securities, on which the government must pay annually in interest some $35 million.
I have tried to show that the budget proposals are less than fair to the small man. Now I intend to show that they are more than generous to the entrenched interests of this country. Nevertheless I do not criticize it in its entirety. Many of the provisions proposed merit the approval of this house: recognition of medical expenses incurred outside of Canada removes an anomaly from the previous budget; allowance of tax deductions to the blind is clearly just; widening of the definition of dependents, and particularly, if I may dare to say so, the inclusion in the definition of illegitimate children, a point I have often raised, is a welcome step; relief to the hard-pressed payers of alimony is also justice; provisions liberalizing the status of superannuation funds, particularly of organized labour, are both necessary and wise. Other features, too, deserve to be commended, but I cannot mention them in my limited time.
I congratulate the government upon the removal of tariffs from farm machinery, but I point out that this step, promised by the Liberals since 1919, is a mincing step, not the giant stride which the situation demands. Farm machinery is monopoly-controlled through the method of "price leadership". I do not think anybody who was on the agriculture committee will deny that. We saw that the prices for farm machinery followed the prices of International Harvester company, which dominates the field on both sides of the border. This is the sort of stubborn fact which the government ought to be facing up to at the present time.
In 1937, when the tariff on farm machinery was reduced, not only did prices to the farmer fail to fall but they actually rose. That is why the parliamentary committee was set up, and the recommendations of that committee still remain to be carried out. Therefore I urge upon the government the necessity of converting some government-owned war-time plant to the peace-time production of farm machinery, under, and this is vital, cooperative ownership, or at least some form of government ownership and control. Only then will the farmer receive his just due in the way of fair prices for machinery.

Turning away from the small man to the other side of the picture, what do we find? We find that the budget contains substantial and, I think, undeserved concessions to big business and an enlargement of those concessions from previous years' budgets. These concessions, I believe, flow from a mistaken philosophy, which says in effect that private enterprise must be cajoled and induced to the point of giving employment. The government is asked to make various tax and tariff concessions, to give monopoly a free hand, in effect to bolster business projects by devious means, to assume the risk of unprofitable ventures itself. This is not free enterprise as it was understood by our forefathers. But appeasement on the part of the government here as elsewhere fails, and returns ultimately to plague the very inventor of it; for, apart altogether from the objection that while the people are called upon to pay the shot it is private interests who stand to make great gains, such appeasement will never succeed in promoting full employment. Even with the help of costly concessions exacted from governments, private enterprise cannot carry the load. National planning and public endeavour must be the keynote of post-war expansion. It will be fruitless and, indeed, costly to engage in attempts to prop up the rotting structure of monopoly capitalism.
The minister states that the taxation treatment of business during the war has been severe. On the surface this appears to be true. There is the excess profits tax. But delving below the surface, the opposite appears to be closer to the truth. Average profits for the four years 1936 to 1939 inclusive are assumed by the Excess Profits Tax Act to be "fair" or standard profits; yet the net income of corporations for the year 1942, the latest for which I could find all the figures available, after payment of all taxes, was twenty-nine per cent higher than this average. My figures were taken from the statistical summary of the Bank of Canada. And over and above war profits as such, business interests are securing indirect war concessions. Through special depreciation they are able to obtain plant and facilities paid for by the people. Through capital assistance they are put in the position of being able to acquire war facilities for little or, in some cases, indeed, for nothing. Through ploughed back war-created profits they are able to increase their capitalization without recourse to new investment from the public. In short, business, but more especially big business, has been digging in during these war years. In this perspective, the various indirect conces-

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
sions to big business contained in the proposed budget ought not to be approved by this house. Considering, too, the prospects for the post-war period, I think we should consider some of the projects that ought to be undertaken in that post-war period, and therefore I will move, seconded by Mr. Gillis:
That the amendment to the motion be further amended by adding thereto the following words:
This house regrets, further, that the government has failed to make provision or plans for the expenditure of, at least, five billion dollars during the first two post-war years for the purpose of establishing a comprehensive national system of social security and of maintaining full employment through public investment in such projects as a low-cost housing programme in town and country, rural electrification, the conversion of government-owned war plants to the production of peace-time goods, the public development of Canada's oil and mineral resources, the promotion of scientific research, and artistic and cultural work throughout Canada.
I move that as an addition to the amendment and therefore as a subamendment to the motion.
In addition to the general appeasement of big business which lies at the heart of the government's policies, what new specific concessions are contained in the budget now proposed? Let us take a look at them. There is, for instance, the proposal that business losses can be chargeable for taxation purposes against profits of the previous year or of the succeeding three years. Perhaps this is desirable in the interests of stability, but we may as well face up to it; it is clearly equivalent in its practical effects to an actual reduction in corporation taxes. That should be understood, and I should like to have the assurance of the government that the farmer will be given at least an equal chance to level out his income for three, four or five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Certainly. He is included.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad to have that assurance from the minister. I took it that it applied to the businessman. The minister's speech was not clear on the point and I am glad to get that assurance, because I believe that is particularly necessary to-day when fluctuations in the farmer's income are often the result of government policy or due to some request made by the government itself.
Looking at some of the other budget concessions, we find that depreciation at double the rates normally allowed is to be permitted in respect of certain investments. Here is another instance of the familiar subsidizing of private enterprises that cannot stand on their own feet. Its plain meaning, as I take it at
100-2744	_ i.1
least, is that the taxpayer is to put up one-half of the new investments but will get nothing in return. The minister will have an opportunity of explaining whether or not my conception of what he proposes is wrong. Let me give another instance, that of deferred maintenance including underground expansion in mines. That is to be deducted from taxes, and that, in my opinion, means that the taxpayer contributes to the cost of operation of private enterprise in that respect. The resolution that dividends of wholly owned subsidiaries of nonresident companies be exempt from taxation is another concession. It seems to me, if I remember the experience of the corporation correctly, that this would, for example enlarge to some extent, if not substantially, the already large profits of Aluminium Limited, which holds a large number of subsidiaries outside Canada.
Again, the resolution allowing the oil industry a tax credit of fifty per cent in respect of new wells is costly and, in my opinion, undeserved. No industry has been more profitable than the oil industry. No industry is entrenched in this country so strongly in its monopolistic position. Imperial Oil, subsidiary of Standard Oil of New Jersey, controls the major portion of the oil industry of this country. A few years ago, according to the price spreads inquiry, it controlled something like ninety per cent of Canada's oil industry. That, however, may have fallen a bit in recent years. Must the public, then, assume the risk of drilling new wells while private shareholders reap all the resulting profits? Is this subsidizing of private interests something that is in the tradition of free enterprise? I say it is not. Can the oil industry, requiring special inducement for the drilling of new wells, be considered as fulfilling its so-called free enterprise function to the community? Research costs may be legitimately deducted from taxable income, and we are doing that for private industry. Will the government give its assurance that public research through some agency such as the national research council will be pushed with all vigour after the war is over? I believe that our national research council and the young scientists associated with it have been virtually starved in recent years. The very best of our young scientists are driven away from our national research organization which ought to be one of the principal means of industrial and economic progress in this country.
I wish to say before I conclude-and my time is now drawing pretty close to its end- something about the prospects of the post-war years. The budget speech recognized how
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

closely interwoven are the war and the afterwar years. I think that is clear, though in my opinion the minister's proposals conspicuously fail to offer a lead toward a solution of the dilemma of our time. That dilemma is the dilemma of want amid actual and potential plenty. Our fighting men deserve the best. They must not be allowed to return to Canada as a part of the world of yesterday. Therefore I say, lest this happen as it happened after the last war, let us prepare now for the expenditure of at least $5,000,000,000 in the two years following the war. Why have I made that suggestion so frequently to this house in the last twc or three years? Because I believe that in planning our post-war activities we should have a target and the assurance that certain moneys will be available and that this parliament is prepared to appropriate them. If we can appropriate, as we are doing this year, more than $5,000,000,000 in one year for the prosecution of the war, then we *ought, as a very minimum, to say that we are going to commit parliament to the expenditure of $5,000,000,000 for the two years following the war. I believe,, if we do that, we [DOT]can get our people to plan comprehensively to meet post-war needs in housing, electrification and all the other things which would improve the standards of life in this country.
I fear the future unless we have comprehensive plans. I believe that some of the countries of the world ar- going to undergo great economic and social upheavals. In spite of what another hon. member said to-day, they are the party promoting revolution. We want to see orderly democratic progress made in our country. That is the purpose for which we organized and the way in which we desire to lead public opinion in this dominion. This expenditure, set beside our war expenditures, seems paltry, but it is, I insist, the minimum figure. It is at least a target to shoot at, something solid on which to hang our hopes for a better Canada to come.
By pledging this we demonstrate the sincerity of our desire to build a new world. The governor of the Bank of Canada and the report of the James committee on reconstruction agree on this; that capital investments of a billion and a half dollars annually must be made in order to achieve jobs for everyone after the war. These are not my opinions. These are the opinions of the chairman of the James committee and the governor of the Bank of Canada. Therefore you see that the suggestion of $5,000,000,000 in two years, which we made two years ago, is not so far beyond the mark as most of our critics suggested when we made it. Private enterprise, by itself,

has not the remotest chance of meeting this total. Even the optimistic forecasts of its propagandists fall far short of it. What is needed is a new freedom to organize production in the public interest. We must bid good-bye to the restrictive practices of orthodox finance and orthodox industry whose only care has been the making of private profit.
Let me quote, Mr. Speaker, from none other than Winston Churchill himself in his 'book, "The World Crisis-The Aftermath." Speaking of the close of the last great war the present Prime Minister of Great Britain had this to say. While I do not agree with all that Mr. Churchill has said or done, I agree with the statement that he made at the close of the last war, which I am going to quote. He said then:
The organization and machinery of which we disposed was powerful and flexible in an extraordinary degree. The able businessmen among us, each the head of a large group of departments, had now been working for a year and a half in a kind of industrial cabinet. They were accustomed to unexpected changes enforced by the shifting fortunes of war. There was very little in the productive sphere they could not, at that time, actually do. A requisition, for instance, for half a million houses would not have seemed more difficult to comply with than those we were already in process of executing for a hundred thousand aeroplanes, or twenty thousand guns, or the medium artillery of the American army, or two million tons of projectiles. But a new set of conditions began to rule from eleven o'clock onwards. The money-cost, which had never been considered by us to be a factor capable of limiting the supply of the armies, asserted a claim to priority from the moment the fighting stopped.
The return of the cabinet to money-cost as the sole governing factor wrecked the dream and the war-time pledge that the British expeditionary force should return in 1918 to "a land fit for heroes." The heroes came back to stagnation and the dole.
In this country we have disregarded the money-costs for the destructive purposes of war. Let us do likewise for the constructive purposes of peace. After all, money is but the medium of exchange. If we fabricate the physical assets, if we can make the commodities, surely we should be able to distribute them among our people and the nations. As has already been said this afternoon, we have to-day one of the most highly trained groups of young men that the world has ever seen. The mechanized army, the men in our air force, have been trained in the operation of machines, in the knowledge of machines, in a manner that no other generation was ever trained. We hope that most of them will come back to us when	the war is	over.	How	are theygoing to live?	They	are	not	going	back	tothe bread lines;	they	are	not	going	back	tofiding the rods;	they	are	not	going	back	to
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
low wage levels upon which they cannot live. The manner in which we have treated the youth of this country who have entered the armed forces, and quite properly so, has given them a new outlook on standards of living. We who travel across this country by rail see the young men and women who before the war would have travelled in the coach, travelling, and rightly so, where they belong, in the sleepers. We see young men and women who would have snatched a lunch at a counter or who would have brought a sandwich-box, go now, and quite rightly, to the dining-car on the train and get a decent meal. We have given our young people a taste of the better standards of life. You cannot bring them back again to the kind of standard of living most of them had before the war began. I see nothing in this budget, and too little in the proposals of the government now before the house, to give any assurance that our standards will be raised willingly when the war ends.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, while one could have advanced other criticism of the budget; while perhaps some of my criticisms will be met in argument from the other side of the house-and I hope they will if in any respect I am wrong-I feel that this is indeed a rich man's budget. It offers a sop to the poor and underprivileged, but on the other hand it contains most valuable concessions to the rich and powerful individuals and corporations who to-day control this land. That, Mr. Speaker, is what I wanted to say.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the two speeches to which we have listened this afternoon have been of a very high order. Generally speaking, I believe we will all agree with the sentiments expressed in them. I am sure each of us was impressed with the closing words of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who said that our boys and girls would not come back to riding the rods. I am afraid too many of us are content with making that statement; but I would venture to wager that if the Liberal government is returned to power, right after the war they will come back to riding the rods, and if they try to do anything about it they will be met with aeroplanes and tear bombs. That is a very gloomy thing to say, but all the evidences I can see in this house and in the banking and commerce committee, where I have had the privilege of serving for some weeks, would indicate to me definitely that there is to be no change which would in any way justify one in expecting that conditions after this war would be any different from those which obtained after the last war.
If I have overlooked any such changes I should be happy to have any government advocate point them out to me.
These are critical and momentous hours in the most critical and momentous period thus far known in our long and eventful history. Signs would indicate that we are now nearing victory and peace. The peace arrangements will provide us with the answer to a burning and insistent question: Is the second world war to have been fought for freedom or for the enslavement of mankind? The tides and winds are all set for the enslavement of our civilization. Unless the financial and economic thinking of our governments changes radically, the enslavement of mankind will be inevitable.
I Shall be be asked, "What factors do you observe which seem to indicate the introduction of slavery for mankind?" There are many such factors, but I shall mention only seven this afternoon.
The first factor is debt. It will be noticed that all the democracies are plunging into debt at a rate that is positively appalling. Those who are in high positions, who carry the responsibility of the war, of course are endeavouring to minimize in the minds of the people the seriousness of the situation. But when the president of our Bank of Canada in his annual report to the minister this year sounded a warning to the minister and the country,-though in a veiled, guarded and conservative manner, I should think that fact ought to be sufficient to indicate that already we are far beyond the safety point in the accumulation of debt.
The second factor is our taxation structure. It is true that this structure has been modified to some extent by the minister after having mercilessly crushed the people of Canada during the last year or two, but the indications are that a system of taxation is being carefully prepared, which can be fixed upon the Canadian people and which will persist for many years after the war. Debt and taxation produce slavery.
The third factor is bureaucracy. It is true that there are complexities in the environment surrounding us which to the ordinary individual make bureaucracy appear a necessity. Certainly we have established in Canada a bureaucracy which should satisfy even Hitler, and which is functioning with smoothness, precision and an irresistible power which I am' sure is quite satisfatory from the point of view of the bureaucrats. The people are becoming accustomed to that sort of government. Bureaucracy may be efficient, but it enslaves.
Another factor which is tending to enslave the world is abundance. One would think that when man invented great machines which.
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

would lift from his shoulders the burdens of life and bring into existence an era of abundance such as his ancestors never even dared dream might be possible, the invention and introduction of such machines would be an introduction to a sort of paradise. Yet what has been the result? The more goods we have been able to produce, the more restricted our lives have become; the more it has become necessary, apparently, to control all those who are engaged in both production and consumption, until now we have a substantial party in the Dominion of Canada advocating, and being listened to while they advocate, complete government ownership of industry. That is being listened to by the Canadian people simply because they are being driven to a species of despair. They are being driven by whom?-by the Liberal party and by their counterparts in other nations. They are being driven by the Progressive Conservative party, because they have not sufficient vitality to suggest any substantial change that would impose even upon a schoolboy.
Consequently the people are going to say, "Well, if there is not anything else we can do about it, I guess we shall have to have government ownership, and anything that goes with it." And so we have the votes for socialism-no, not for socialism, exactly, but for something different from the horrible things the people have been enduring for the last fifteen years.
What is the reason? Abundance. Abundance can crush a people, unless those people know how to distribute that abundance. .During the war our ability to produce abundance has been enhanced surprisingly. I believe it was Doctor Charles A. A. Stein who, within the last two years, said that, since war broke out, the amount of raw materials available in the United States had increased between ten and one hundred times. That is simply because new processes have been discovered, as a result of which men are able to make almost anything out of almost anything. At the same time increased skill in the management of machines and technological processes has taught men how to use these new continents of matters which have been discovered for the fabrication of abundance. But up to the present time, astonishing as it may. seem, no one has been able to get the ear of any substantial number of people with any proposal as to how to distribute that abundance. This strikes me with .the deepest apprehension.
IMr. Blackmore.]
Another factor tending toward the enslavement of man is this very inability to distribute. And I think, too, that worse than the inability to distribute is the impatience which I notice when I undertake to discuss with the average group of people anything pertaining to distribution. People seem to think it does not count. Well, it does count. The ability to distribute does count.
Another matter which in my judgment is threatening enslavement is the fact that our people generally throughout the country are so completely unfamiliar with the new and strange conditions confronting them, that they do not know what it is all about. They are unfamiliar with the essential changes which have taken place. How rarely do we hear in the house, for example, any sober exposition of the impact of machines upon our economy? I believe this year the only member who has been sufficiently intrepid to discuss the matter has been the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Kuhl); and he has been rewarded for his pains by at least half a dozen offensive remarks.
Why is it that we do not hear government members discussing the seriousness of the impact of machines upon our economy? Sometime between 1913 and 1928 we rounded some mighty corner in this world. We left an age of scarcity and sped into an age of abundance. Nevertheless we hear no serious discussion of the matter among members of the Progressive Conservative party, and there is no reference to it at all by the Liberals. And yet these two groups constitute by far the majority of members in the house.
Why is there so much indifference in respect of these important matters? It must be that there is an indifference among the - people in the constituencies represented by those hon. members. The people, generally, are unfamiliar with the adjustments which can and should be made to meet the new situation. They are unfamiliar with the educational equipment necessary to enable a democratic people to judge of the soundness of the various proposals available to them. Hon. members will find something of thought-provoking quality in the Ottawa Citizen of June 28 where, at page 2, appears an article respecting a survey conducted by the Canadian institute of public opinion. It appears under the heading, "What is the meaning of inflation? But few Canadians have the answer." We read that a careful survey was made of the people respecting the matter of inflation. Even among people with complete college educa-

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
tions only thirty-three per cent had good answers; another twenty-eight per cent had only fair answers and the remainder were absolutely wrong as to the meaning of inflation.
Then, coming down through the various groups, including the college group, incomplete; high school, complete and incomplete; public school, complete and incomplete, we find the people displaying an alarming ignorance on the question: What is inflation? Some members will ask: "What bearing has that on the subject you are discussing?" Well, the bearing it has on the subject is simply this, that the very moment anyone suggests a monetary solution as being the way out, he is immediately met with the statement, "This will cause inflation." Then the rank and file of the people, not knowing anything at all about what inflation is, or how it is caused or how it can be controlled, are deluded by clever political advocates-and I shall use that word, to be charitable. The result is that we remain in danger. A very serious element in the threat of enslavement is the lack of information which prevails among' the Canadian people, and to an equal degree, probably, among the peoples in other democratic countries.
Another influence working for the enslavement of man is that in all the democracies the political parties, generally speaking, are endeavouring not to give the people the truth, but rather to deceive them. I have commented on this matter in times past. You hear Liberals devoting most of their time to extolling the virtues of trade. Any informed man knows that the possibilities of trade as a means of solving the problems which present themselves to-day are exceedingly limited. Therefore he should inform his constitutents, but he does not. He deceives them. He leads them to believe that the raising or lowering of tariffs is a panacea which will cure the ills confronting them. Any well informed man must know that the effect which tariffs have on the solution of our problem is extremely negligible. So that we have people being deceived.
In addition to that we have world agencies, such as international finance, definitely working for the enslavement of mankind through world organization. Such agencies are advocating economic planning and socialism as a means of obtaining security. They receive support simply because they promise security. They advocate a world police force because people can be deluded into thinking that a police force will mean peace. They advocate monetary stabilization because people can be deluded into thinking that monetary stabilization will greatly facilitate trade. These international organizations are working with an elaborate, highly organized propaganda machine.
I have named the several factors which are threatening to destroy the freedom of man. What is the present government offering as a solution? Nothing. What does the present budget offer by way of a solution? Nothing. All that this government is able to propose is an increase in debt or an increase in taxation. It talks about increasing international trade. I shall have something to say about this later on. The King government can conceive of no method of distribution except that of international trade. That is all we hear spoken of by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his supporters. This means that they advocate a struggle for favourable trade balances, which means that they advocate a resort to a system under which each of fifty odd nations must sell more than it buys.
Mr. ILSLEY; Why does the hon. gentleman say that?

speechtext: Because without a favourable trade balance it is impossible for them to carry on. Is it not so? As far as I have been able to gather from the remarks I have heard, there has to be a favourable trade balance.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: It does not.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: International trade is a system that has failed to distribute and has involved us in war after war.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is just a typical Liberal question. Liberals can see no other way of distributing. The question supports completely what I am saying.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I shall have something to say about that before I have finished; all things in their place. The simple fact of the matter is that the Liberals know of no way of distributing except through international trade. When that breaks down, their whole distributive machinery breaks down.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What will you do with your surplus production?
The Budget-Mr. Blackmon

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I shall have something to say about that; all things in their place. I am saying that international trade cannot be relied upon as an adequate means of distributing. This has involved us in war after war.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would you distribute where there is no nation?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The other day when discussing reconstruction the Prime Minister named several of the committees which had been appointed by his government to study reconstruction. I wonder how many of us have read the recommendations of those various committees. If we have, I think we shall be astounded at the lack of anything constructive in those recommendations. They have simply added to the difficulty which has been created already by insincerity in the house. The obscurity and insincerity of parliamentary debate have served to confuse and confound the people of Canada. It is the solemn duty of parliament to give the people light. Party politicians have in fact left them in all-embracing darkness and fog. In these circumstances, therefore, it is natural that the people should swing from one extreme to the other, from the orthodoxy of capitalism to the orthodoxy of socialism. It is the duty of Canadian leadership to show the people that both of these orthodox ways are false and that the true way must be based on freedom. In either of these false orthodox ways there is no freedom. To have economic security Canadians must reform capitalism. To have freedom, Canadians must retain freedom of enterprise, freedom of speech, freedom of action, freedom for the obscure people as well as for the prominent.
In the report of each and every one of the committees on reconstruction appointed by the Mackenzie King government there is a blind adherence to obsolete and bankrupt formulas. There is not a hint of change. The voice of each committee sounds like the voice of big business speaking through its mouthpiece, the Prime Minister of Canada. If individual enterprise is to be bound to function under the restraints and prohibitions imposed upon it by the present government of Canada, then individual enterprise will, indeed, be short lived.
Individual enterprise under a reformed monetary system would have the power to give greater security than has socialism. And such security it can give without impairment of individual freedom. It must be the duty of every lover of democracy to fight to liberate our system of individual enterprise from

the prison house of international finance so that it may bring the people the security to which they are entitled.
Wherein lies the key to the solution of our perplexing problems? A minute ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) asked what we would do. I am going to speak in general terms, but I think my words will clearly indicate the solution. It lies in the adequate use of the national credit of each of the various individual nations. What is the essential nature of our problem? It is how to distribute. Mankind has learned how to produce what mankind requires. - What men mu,st learn is where and how to obtain purchasing power and how to distribute that purchasing power among the people and among the nations.
Then the consumers will be able to buy their needs; the producers will be able to sell their products. The wholesale textile association of Great Britain, in the second report of the post-war reconstruction committee on international finance, issued in March, 1944, quotes Sumner Welles as saying on March 30, 1942:
The problem which will confront us when the years of the post-war period are reached is not primarily one of production. For the world can readily produce what mankind requires. The problem is rather one of distribution and purchasing power, of providing the mechanism whereby what the world produces may be fairly distributed among the nations of the world, and of providing the means whereby the people of the world may obtain the world's goods and services.
Where now can money or purchasing power be obtained without additional taxation, without additional debt? Money can be created by the government of any sovereign state as,, for example, Canada created $26,000,000 and spent it into circulation in the last war, or as the United States in time of distress created greenbacks. I am not advocating that money be created by printing bills. There are other ways. But the principle of creating national currency debt-free is the principle upon which, a new economy and a new order must be based. The amount of such money that can be safely created and used by any state depends upon the goods and services which that state can produce and consume. A number of members have been struggling in the banking and commerce committee to get a little light to shine on the pages of the proceedings of that committee. I believe that we have succeeded in establishing that fact.

definitely that the government produce the currency and distribute the currency, and the currency "will / enable the people to buy the goods produced, thereby providing a market, providing distribution and providing consumption. speechtext: If I may say so, there has been a great deal of ambiguous talk that one finds it hard to understand, and I just wanted to pin the hon. member down on a certain point. Now I am satisfied. Thank you.

speechtext: You have never had any difficulty in "pinning me down" on that point. I have said that thing with clarity at least one hundred times since I have been in the house, so that the poor wayfaring man, though a fool, need not err therein. Any state by increasing its production and consumption can increase the amount of money it can have, and the amount of money which it can have depends on the goods and services which it can produce and consume. Thus obviously, the state can increase its revenues by increasing its goods and services.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It does not produce all the goods and services which the people require-

speechtext: I realize the difficulties which lie in the way. Let me say this to the minister. The moment any person offers a suggestion you look at the difficulties. We grant the difficulties. But how many difficulties are there in the way of your trade proposals or any other proposals? Study the two together and see under which set of proposals you have the better chance of coming through.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On what basis would this currency be distributed?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On this basis, that the object of the government would be to enable the people to buy enough of the goods they are able to produce.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: By what means?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Through modifications of price and modifications of income. Those are two adjustments which I should be glad to elaborate to the satisfaction of the hon. member. But I have not the time now. I have only forty minutes. I am talking against time. But that is the solution and the method. The state increases the income in the hands of the people, income which they will spend to enable them to purchase their needs from what they produce.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The question is, how?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You do it through two devices, by modification of price and by modification of income. You had an example of modification of income in the Prime Minister's proposal to give family allowances. There is a modification of income. Anyone with the intelligence of a member of parliament should be able to go further and work the whole thing out.
The debt-free money available to the government of any state can be used, just as I have told the hon. member, to modify the price structure in that state-raise prices that need to be raised and lower prices that need to be lowered-and to increase the income in the hands of its people. The whole thing is done by the use of debGfree money.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Debt-free money is the answer.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Debt-free money is the key to the solution. It is the basis upon which the whole thing can be worked out. My hon. friend is a doctor, is he not?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I used to be.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He knows what a tremendous amount depended upon the discovery of anaesthetics.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Quite so.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the discovery of anaesthetics you had a great principle on which you could work. When you discovered that principle you could build upon it. The principle of debt-free money is a principle upon which you can work. Your money can be used to modify the price structure in the state and to increase the income in the hands of the people. Thus internal distribution can be provided for. That is the answer to the question of the Minister of Agriculture. International distribution can be effected by Mutual Aid arrangements, and Mutual Aid can be financed in considerable measure with debt-free money created by the state and spent into circulation, without any increase in debt and without any increase in taxation. Just as soon as the
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

governments of the world come to understand that, they will not be afraid of increasing and elaborating their Mutual Aid agreements to the extent that the international distribution of goods will be based upon mutually acceptable arrangements rather than upon cut-throat competition, which works to the disadvantage of the weakest nations, the ones most in need of trade. Through cut-throat competition they lose their trade.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Finally your solution consists in the distribution of debt-free money?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, the distribution of debt-free money up to the limit of the nation's capacities to absorb that debt-free money by reason of the goods and services which the nation produces. That money is used in raising the standard of living in the economy.
Thus Mutual Aid can be extended to the degree necessary to enable all peoples to be free from want and free from fear. Thus trade rivalry can be reduced and eliminated, and thus the main cause of war can be removed.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the government call in one of these many committees on reconstruction, perhaps the present reconstruction committee of the House of Commons, and say to the chairman, " Now look here, you are perfectly at liberty to call witnesses and examine papers to discover whether or not there is any validity in this contention of monetary reform. Go into the matter with very great care and call in as witnesses the men who know about it."

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We called Douglas the last time.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And he would have done an extremely good job, but for men like Hackett who did everything they could to hurt him and prevent his voice from being heard. If you call men like Douglas and have a committee that is sympathetic and ready to learn, and that is not trying to destroy him politically, not trying to get some little thing which it can magnify out of all proportion as certain Liberal members on the banking and commerce committee are doing to-day, you will learn a great deal of truth. I suggest that the government adopt that policy with at least two or three of these committees on reconstruction, and I guarantee that within a year they will have a great deal more light on this vexatious problem of distribution than they have to-day.
The governor of the Bank of Canada in his annual report has indicated what the possibilities would be if we began to create money

to represent the tremendous capacity for production which we shall have immediately at the close of the war. I commend to hon. members the remarks made by the governor of the Bank of Canada on page 11 of his annual report to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). He says:
By the end of 1943 the gainfully occupied population had risen to approximately 5,100.000 but about 1,900,000 of these were engaged in the armed forces, in supplying the weapons of war, or in producing the food required for special war-time exports. The number available to meet civilian needs had therefore fallen to about 3,200,000, but at the same time the average standard of living had risen materially and was probably higher than it had ever been.
How serious that is, and imagine what will happen when the others return and are producing goods themselves!

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I wish to say, first, that I am sure we all greatly appreciate what has been accomplished by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). His accomplishment has made it possible for Canada to carry on a war effort which has brought praise from outstanding men in all the allied nations. The Minister of Finance has indeed proved himself a great financier. To raise eight billions of dollars loaned from the people of Canada would appear almost an impossibility for a country' with the population that we have, and it is indeed a great achievement. Notwithstanding this, the people of Canada are better off financially than they have ever been. I am informed that the savings accounts to-day are two and a half 'billions as compared with one and a half billions when the war began.
The one dark spot in Canada's war effort has been the lack of cooperation the government has received from some members of the opposition parties. It is indeed a sad thing in time of war that men cannot forget their politics and give the government some cooperation. We have been here now for five months and it looks as though we shall be here two or three months longer, when many of us should be at home doing more useful work. I am sure the people of Canada do Aot appreciate the actions of some members of the opposition parties.

The Budget-Mr. Farquhar
I wish to speak to-night for a short time on what is, to my mind, a dangerous policy which is being advocated in this country, at the present time, and the seriousness of which I feel is not full}" realized. I refer to the policy advocated by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party as it affects the country generally and especially as it affects the farmers and organized labour. Some members of the C.C.F. party go so far as to deny that their policy includes the socialization of farms. Whether that is their policy or not, I think we have sufficient evidence to prove that at least a great many workers and organizers of the C.C.F. party are advocating and admitting frankly that the nationalization of farms is C.C.F. policy. A short time ago I met a C.C.F. organizer and he frankly admitted to me that the socialization of farms was their policy. I said to him, "You are not frank enough to admit that when you go into a farming community." He replied, "Well, that is our policy." A short time after that-and this happened recently.-I met another C.C.F. organizer and I put the same question to him. He said, "Well, we do believe in collective farming," and he admitted that this eventually would mean the socialization of farms.
Again, a prominent man, Mr. Levans, member of the legislature for Woodbine, Toronto, is reported to have said, at a banquet in Orillia, that the farmers could remain on their farms during their lifetime but could not sell or will their farms to anyone else. And again, we have the leader of the C.C.F. party who, when asked in Maclean's magazine the question, "Do you believe the state should operate everything?" answered, "Practically everything." Well, as farming is Canada's greatest industry, surely "practically everything" includes farming.
Any man to-day who discusses this question with C.C.F. workers will agree with me that they frankly admit that this is C.C.F. policy. Therefore, whether some members of this house agree to that or not, nevertheless the rank and file of the C.C.F. party do believe in it and frankly admit that it is C.C.F. policy. Again, the leader of the C.C.F. party is quoted in Maclean's as saying, when asked the question, "Will the. C.C.F. party control labour?"- "Yes." Just how does the C.C.F. party intend to control labour? It will control labour by making labour organizations ineffective.
I am sure we all agree that over the last half century labour has done a great deal in bringing about better working and living conditions. Labour, it is true, has had a hard fight over the last half century to accomplish what it has. We all agree that labour has done a great deal for the labouring man. It is true
that labour has not always had good leadership. Labour has often been wrongly advised, but that is no argument against labour policies. That also has been true of organized industry. Industry has also very often had very bad leadership, which has led to a great deal of trouble.
Organized labour and organized industry are learning that if they are to avoid the experiences of the past they must have a better understanding, and that can be brought about only by better cooperation, union recognition and compulsory collective bargaining. If the C.C.F. policies were put into effect, there is not a class in Canada which would be so seriously affected as organized labour. All the hard work they have done over past years, everything they have accomplished, all the sacrifices they have made would be lost effort. It could not be any other way where industries were owned and operated by the government. Is there a man in organized labour who believes that if the government owned all industries in the country the government would allow him to continue to organize and to continue to strike and to defy the government? I wonder if any man who belongs to organized labour believes that. If he does he will learn that he is making a great mistake. When I make that statement I think I hear someone say, "What about industries which are already being operated by the government?" That is easily explained. Take, for instance, the railways. One is owned by the government and another by a private company. The men who are working on these two roads belong to one organization, and just as long as the men who are working on the government-owned road belong to the same organization as the men who are working on the privately-owned road they must receive the same consideration; but if the government took over all the railroads in Canada that would place them in a much different position. If the government took over all the railroads and the men went out on strike what would happen? Well, what would happen would be just what was about to happen recently in another country where there was talk of the government taking over the roads. They would put the officials of the company in uniform and turn the operating of the roads over to the national defence department. No government in power dare allow any organization to defy it. Just as long as any government is operating an industry, labour has not its freedom. I thought I heard someone say that if the C.C.F. were in power they would not treat labour in that way; that they are too much interested in organized labour to treat it in that manner. That may or may
The Budget-Mr. Farquhar

not be true. It matters very little whether it is true or not because governments come and governments go. Any government that would take office after the C.C.F. government were in power would have to continue to operate the industries taken over by the C.C.F government. They could not hand them back again to private companies. They would have to continue to operate those industries. The government following the C.C.F, might possibly be a Progressive Conservative government, although that is not likely. It might be a Social Credit government, or it might be a Bloc Populaire, or some other form of government; but, as I say, it matters not what government succeeds a C.C.F. government, it must continue to operate the industries that are taken over by the C.C.F. government. Is organized labour going to hand over its organization to the mercy of any government that might come into power? I wonder. I wonder whether labour has stopped to realize just what might happen to it under any government which might come into power? They would be entirely at the mercy of the government because they would not have their freedom under government ownership. I have spent many years of my life working in the interests of organized labour. I have taken part in long and bitter strikes, one strike lasting nine months, which won for the miners of British Columbia the first eight-hour day that they ever enjoyed. An eight-hour day is a long day for miners to work underground in the conditions under which they have to work. I know something of the long and bitter experience that labour has passed through, and I know something of the sacrifice they have made in order that they might better their working and living conditions.
As one who has the cause of labour at heart I appeal to organized labour to let no government control their organization to the extent it would if it owned and operated the industries in which they are working. I would recommend to labour that they think over very carefully the recommendations for the post-war world issued by the American federation of labour, which reads as follows:
Free enterprise is an essential part of the democratic way of life. We believe wholeheartedly in free enterprise as an essential in personal freedom. Free enterprise and free labour are interdependent; neither can last without the other.
Those are not my words, Mr. Speaker. This is a recommendation passed by the American federation of labour and sent on to their locals. It is a true statement. Labour can never be free while the government of the country owns and operates the industries in which labour is

working. I appeal to labour representatives in this house and in the country to think this over very seriously. Labour cannot retain its freedom if the industries are operated by the government and controlled through state socialism.
Another danger that I see is in the class of men who are getting into the C.C.F. party and who will eventually control it. I have been through the mill and I see clearly what is happening in the ranks of the C.C.F. party to-day. Perhaps some of the older members of the house will remember the days of the
O.B.U., the One Big Union. I belonged to the Sandon branch of the western federation of miners in British Columbia. It was a strong branch and had a very large membership. We owned our own block, a large one, containing a large auditorium and fraternity hall. We had stores rented on the ground floor. We owned our own hospital employed our own doctor and nurses. Members of the One Big Union worked into our organization. They became so numerous that they outvoted us and took our property from us. That is exactly what is happening in the C.C.F. today. The class of men who are coming into the C.C J1. party to-day will eventually and before very long control and dictate the policies of that party. It is all very well for the leader of the CCF. (Mr. Coldwell) to make the statement that he quite often does to the effect that they are not going to take in progressive labour, which is communist. I wish to tell the leader of the C.C.F. that they are taking them in by the hundreds. And they cannot prevent them from coming in. They will do exactly what they did in our organization. Very shortly they will control and dictate the policies of the party. No one realizes that better than the leader of the C.C.F. party. No one sees that danger coming more clearly than he does. If he continues in the moderate way he has spoken from time to time, very soon that class will be asking him to step aside and make way for a more radical type of leadership. Do not misunderstand me,. Mr. Speaker. I am not doubting the sincerity of the leader of the C.C.F. party. Many of the principles they advocate I have supported all my life. What I do oppose is the method by which they are trying to bring those principles into effect. They talk about destroying monopolies. You cannot destroy monopolies by creating greater monopolies, and that is exactly what the C.C.F. would do if they came into power. The nationalization of industry will create the greatest monopoly Canada has ever experienced. We know very well how this has worked out in other countries, and we know it can work out in only one way in any

The Budget-Mr. Itoss (Souris)
[DOT]country. I believe in a certain amount of ' control. I believe that anyone who tries to take advantage of anyone else should be controlled. I trust that this war has brought us to a greater realization of our duty toward our fellow men than we have ever had before. You will remember how men piled up millions during the last war. That has not been done [DOT]during this war. I hope that the day of the millionaire is gone forever, and that never again will the moneyed interests of this country control its affairs, as they have in the past. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I believe in control where necessary, but I do not want to lose my freedom through state socialism.
Only one class will benefit under a C.C.F. government. I refer to the class that never did have and never will have any stake in this country unless they get it from someone else. I refer to the class that has fought labour organizations ever since labour began to organize. I refer to the class against whom labour men have had to picket in order to prevent them from taking their jobs when they were on strike. I refer to the class who believe that Canada owes them a living and that it is not necessary to work for it. That class now see an opportunity of getting something for nothing, and they are going to take advantage of that opportunity if they can.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that I stand for a square deal to the labouring classes, whether on the farm or in the factory. Let us beware of any party which advocates government ownership of farms or factories. If that policy should be put into effect it will be the saddest day labour in Canada has ever experienced.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my appreciation of the manner in -which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) presented his budget proposals and the estimates of our cash requirements for the coming year, amounting to some six billion dollars, an all-time high in the history of this county. We realize that the hon. gentleman has a very difficult task, and I /should like to express the hope that his health may be spared while he has this task in hand and, of course, for a long time after that,
I disagree in principle with several of the proposals enunciated by the minister. I should like to compliment my colleague the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) who, as official critic of the budget, dealt -with it this afternoon in an able manner. I wish especially to endorse his tribute to the gallant men and women of the armed forces who today are doing such a magnificent job for us in attempting to preserve all the worth-while
things of our way of life, and also to those people on the home front in this country, engaged in agriculture and industry, who are so ably supporting our fighting forces.
I believe there is a great deal of wasteful extravagance in Canada at the present time under this government. As an example I mention the wartime information board, which I believe spends approximately $1,000,000 annually. A great deal of the information it distributes is political propaganda, some of it false and misleading. Someone may say, "Give us an example of that." I would refer anyone interested to page 26 of the January, 1944, issue of "Canada at War" dealing with the men available in the Quebec military district between the ages of eighteen and forty-five. That information is not correct. I would mention also page 55 of the May, 1944, issue of the same booklet, which contains false information with respect to Japanese nationals in Canada. Both these matters have been dealt with already by other hon. members.
During these years of war huge amounts of money have been spent in the purchase of properties for industrial plants, air training centres and so on. Apparently there has not been a uniform system of valuation in connection with the purchase of these properties. There are other, larger items with which I shall deal at a later stage of my remarks. In the matter of income tax, I am definitely of the opinion that exemptions should be increased to at least $800 for single persons and $1,600 for married men. I believe also that a farmer and his wife, who helps him on the farm, should be granted exemptions on the same basis that they are granted to the man and his wife who work in industry or any other occupation. The present discrimination in this respect is wholly unjustified. In the past the receipts from all live stock sold within the calendar year have been classed as income, which is very unfair. In the case of breeding herds especially I believe a percentage should be allowed as capital. In connection with the power required to operate a farm, the money received from the sale of any horses is classed as income, while a tractor is allowed as capital, along with other equipment, I have never been able to see the justification for that discrimination. Then the income of farmers should be averaged over a period of years. This is something for which I have asked during every budget debate since I came here in 1940. Last year the minister announced that the income of a farmer might be averaged Over two years, but I believe the period should be six years so that losses in certain seasons could be offset by profits in others. This is now done

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Souris)
over a five-year period in Great Britain, where the hazards of farming are not normally as great as in Canada.
Another point I should like to emphasize is that if a person overpays the amount of tax due, no interest is allowed on this overpayment when the refund is made. On the other hand, if a person inadvertently pays less than he should, the department assesses a rather severe penalty plus interest. Surely, as a matter of justice it should work both ways; if the government have the use of the money they should allow interest on making the rebate.
The present tax return form is too complicated and should be simplified in some manner. It is altogether too difficult for the average taxpayer.
Under the wartime prices and trade board we hear a great deal about agricultural subsidies. I maintain that in reality these are consumer subsidies, and that in many cases the primary producers are carrying much more than their fair share. Especially is that true in respect of beef and grain.
As an example of ceiling prices and controls I would cite that of fuel wood. We had an example shown to us where the ceiling price for poplar wood at the head of the lakes in Ontario was $7.50 a cord. In Manitoba for the same wood the price was $5.50 a cord, including $1 bonus. There are corresponding differences in respect of other types of wood. This wood was shipped from the head of the lakes to Winnipeg with a freight rate of $8 a cord, as paid for through government subsidies. This wood, which cost $15.50 a cord, was shipped through a wooded area in Manitoba and sold in Winnipeg for $5.15.
That is one glaring example of our present controls and inefficiencies. The secretary of agriculture of the United States states that in that country a peace-time farm production of fifty per cent more than pre-war level is possible. Canada's basic industry has often been stated to be and actually is agriculture. Prosperous basic industries are essential for the prosperity of the nation. Agriculture is an industry engaged in the manufacture of foodstuffs. It is an industry which has approximately 735,000 branch factories across Canada, with each factory facing problems similar to those found in all other industrial enterprises. The farmer, like the manufacturer in the operation of his factory, is faced with problems of management, labour, working capital, adequate power supply, overhead costs, finance, factoiy efficiency, sales promotion and markets.

It is in an examination of these that we get to the root of our agricultural problem. This industry of agriculture embraces some 3,163,280 people who live on the land. A farm, whether small or large, is an individual capitalistic enterprise. I think it is important that we should appreciate that situation at this time. During the past year agricultural production, with an approximate decrease of twenty-five per cent in man-power, had well over a forty per cent increase in foodstuffs, all of which are required in the prosecution of the war. The war supplies furnished to Great Britain under Mutual Aid have included all types of supplies, procured for Great Britain through Canadian government departments or agencies. They bought huge tonnages of wheat, flour, bacon, beef, cheese, eggs and various other special farm products. Mutual Aid has been extended to cover Canada's contribution to the united nations relief and rehabilitation administration, known as UNRRA. This will take us into the post-war period.
Many people ask, then, what about the future of agriculture? Nutritional standards, and the improvement thereof, will create greater demands for agricultural foodstuffs. Nutrition surveys carried out across Canada have shown serious diet deficiencies among more than half the families of Canada. Half a million Canadian children are undernourished. It is now internationally recognized that there must be increased consumption of adequate quantities of nutritional food. Agriculture has suffered more than any other activity in Canada from lop-sided development. The Sirois commission report states definitely that from 1896 to 1913, under a vigorous immigration policy by the governments of the day, assisted by land companies and railway companies, a tremendous expansion took place in territories of Canada. Settlement took place without discrimination. The territories settled grew from about 10,000,000 acres to some 70,000,000 acres in that period. The production of wheat was increased from approximately 20,000,000 bushels to some 210,000,000 bushels during that period. Since that time production has again almost doubled.
During that period of time no encouragement was given to industrialists and tradesmen to come to this country and develop industry. We have greater undeveloped natural resources in Canada than are to be found in any other country of the world. We have great facilities for the development of industry. If in this country there had been a balanced programme of immigration and development we would enjoy a market within Canada for very much of our agricultural production.

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Souris)
For example, statistics prove that for the year 1937 the family of the average industrial employee consumed agricultural products to the extent of $409.35 annually. These figures for to-day would be considerably higher. On this basis, if we had 5,000,000 heads of families employed in industry there would be an immediate home market in Canada for our present agricultural production.
I am one who thinks that in a country such as Canada, with our vast undeveloped natural resources, our very cheap electrical power and the possibility for further development of cheap electrical power, we must have, during the generation following the end of the present war, a much greater development of peace-time industry. This would create employment for all our ex-service men and for every able-bodied Canadian willing to work. It would also necessitate an immigration policy on a selective basis for industrial development-not land settlement, as in the past. This could be had at a greater remuneration for employees than has been customary in the past history of Canada.
In that great and comparatively new and cosmopolitan country to the south of us, the United States of America, we find an example where, prior to this war, many of our young and trained men left Canada and received much greater remuneration in the United States than they could receive in this country, their native land.
In this respect there is a real field of work for the new Department of Reconstruction. I trust it will follow the suggestion through. Many of the new Canadians, or those of foreign ancestry, have splendid war records, when compared with the records of many native-born Canadians. The real native-born Canadians are those of French Canada, or Quebec. French Canada is approximately 300 years old, yet it is still a young and vigorous country. These people are possessed of material, economic and spiritual ideals which are worth fighting for, and which would develop a strong and united Canada. They, and more especially the generation for twenty-five years prior to 1939, have received false or improper leadership with respect to citizenship in this country.
In this connection I should like to quote from a speech by the Prime Minister (Mr Mackenzie King) delivered in this house on March 30, 1939, and reported at page 2419 of Hansard. It states:
Canada, it is contended, is not a country of unlimited powers; it has not the capacity to stand indefinite strains. We have tremendous tasks to do at home, in housing the people, in caring for the aged and helpless, in relieving drouth and unemployment, in building roads,
in meeting our heavy burden of debt, in making provision for Canada's defence, and in bringing our standards of living and civilization to the levels our knowledge now makes possible. There is no great margin of realizable wealth for this purpose; we must to a greater or less extent, choose between keeping our own house in order, and trying to save Europe and Asia.
