The idea that every twenty years this country should automatically and as a matter of course take part in a war overseas for democracy or self-determination of other small nations, that a country which has all it can do to run itself should feel called upon to save, periodically, a continent that cannot run itself, and to these ends risk the lives of its people, risk bankruptcy and political disunion, seems to many a nightmare and sheer madness.
Then in the same speech, as reported at page 2426 of Hansard, he said:
One strategic fact is clear: the days of great expeditionary forces of infantry crossing the oceans are not likely to recur. Two years ago, I expressed in this house the view that it was extremely doubtful if any of the British dominions would ever send another expeditionary force to Europe.
That was the Prime Minister speaking a few months before the declaration of war. He went on to say:
One political fact is equally clear: in a war to save the liberty of others, and thus our own, we should not sacrifice our own liberty or our own unity. Planning and coordination would be essential, but the necessary coordination could be made, and if this government were in power it would be made, without sacrificing those vital ends and conditions of our existence. Profits could and would be rigidly controlled, and profiteering suppressed. But men's lives and men's wills cannot be put on the same basis as goods and profits. The present government believes that conscription of men for overseas service would not be a necessary or an effective step. Let me say that so long as this government may be in power, no such measure will be enacted.
As I pointed out, that was a few months before the declaration of war. In 1939 there was a declaration of the same policy that had been practised by the same leader and some of his cohorts for twenty-five years, while this generation was growing up. Little wonder that when the thirty-day training scheme was introduced during the early stages of this war the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said that this was necessary in order to impress Canadian youth with the duty of citizenship. This generation, especially those of the province of Quebec, believe that they have been deceived. There are many splendid fighting troops from Quebec. I prefer to believe that recent events have so challenged the people of this nation that the views expressed by that fighting padre of French Canada, Father Armand Sabourin of Les Fusiliers

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Souris)
Mount-Royal, are more indicative of what all people are thinking across Canada to-day. He said on his return from Dieppe:
We wanted to prevent Hitler from reaching our shores to-morrow to destroy our faith, our tongue and our institutions. We crossed the channel to fight with England for Canada. If I am a free man to-day in my country I owe it to England. The Anglo-Protestant government recognizes my rights as a French Canadian and gives me complete freedom of religion and of speech and respects my traditions. That is why we went to Dieppe.
I believe that with proper leadership French Canada would do their part in creating and developing a great united Canada. I believe that is yet more than possible.
We have in Canada to-day a serious manpower problem. A few weeks ago the Minister of National Defence assured us that we had adequate reserves for our army to meet battle *casualties. Those are his exact words which may be found in Hansard. To-day under his authority the chief recruiting officer of the Department of National Defence says that we are in urgent need of forty-eight thousand reinforcements for overseas. He attempts to shame men from industry and other vocations into enlisting. At the same time the farmer has to do without help. According to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) we are
196,000	men short in industry.
In the face of all this we have an army of approximately 75,000 now in service for the defence of Canada. This home army represents a cost of $150,000,000 a year. Seventy-five thousand men are kept out of agriculture, out of industry, out of the war, out of everything but the public treasury. The farmer and his wife along with other citizens of Canada work many long hours in order to pay for this. The government has access to information as to where these men are required most, and yet they, the responsible ministers, apparently refuse to act. In fairness to some of the men of the home defence army to whom I have talked I think I should say that they make the statement that the responsible ministers of the government have available to them certain information. If they or the government refuse to state and take proper action as to where these men can best serve, that is their problem.
We have the strange anomaly of several ministers on the front benches, family men . with good records in the last war, under the cloak of political expediency, as many people [DOT]claim, submitting to the whims of their leader the present Prime Minister on man-power. We have had set forth by two great world leaders. Prime Minister Churchill and President Roosevelt, the Atlantic charter for the 
four freedoms. That is what we desire and what we should strive for.
Mr. Speaker, I take second place to no man in my dislike of war. Neither do I take second place to any person with respect to my interest in the welfare of humanity. At the same time I trust I have some realization of my duty as a citizen of Canada. I shall support the amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), which reads as follows:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets-
(a)	that no adequate steps have been taken to simplify the forms and modernize the methods of taxation;
(b)	that no effective action has been taken to grant a measure of relief to the men and women in the lower income brackets by raising the exemption in income tax for single persons to not less than $800 per annum and for married persons to not less than $1,600 per annum;
(c)	that no provision has been made to encourage greater war-time production by exempting overtime pay from income tax;
(d)	that sufficient provision has not been made for the elimination of the inequities presently existing with respect to agricultural taxation:
(e)	that no adequate provision has been made to ensure increased post-war employment through the discovery and development of metallic and non-metallic mineral resources;
(f)	that the government has failed to make effective the full mobilization of our financial, industrial and material resources, as well as our man-power, but is maintaining a so-called home defence army, at a cost to the taxpayer in excess of $150 million per annum, at a time when the need for men for army reinforcements, for farming and for industry is so urgent."
I trust that we shall not forget that at this moment young men are fighting for our way of life and for this parliament. I think that should at all times be our first consideration. As my colleague pointed out this afternoon, many of these gallant young men will not return to us. Many others will return maimed for life. They and their dependents must be our first care at all times.
Just before I close I should like to make some reference to procedure in this house. The statement has often been made that the length of the session depends on the opposition. I have taken some pains to check Hansard on certain points. I remember one to me rather disgraceful day in this house, Tuesday, April 25, when we wasted the entire day on the report of the special committee on the revision of standing orders of this house. We made no progress whatever. Some twenty members on the government side spoke in that debate, three Progressive Conservatives, five C.C.F., three Social Credit and two others. Fifty pages of Hansard were filled on that

The Budget-Mr. Dorion
day, or approximately 5,500 lines. Of this amount 4,463 lines, or over eighty per cent, were taken by the government speakers; 449 lines by the Progressive Conservatives and 354 lines by the C.C.F.
Then we had a motion from the Prime Minister to the effect that Wednesday sittings of the house were out from February 22 to June 14, 1944, in spite of most strenuous opposition from all opposition parties in the house.
We have also had the banking and commerce committee sitting for some twenty-seven days, and almost the entire time of that committee has been monopolized by two members of the government party.
There are many other figures I could give of the time that has been taken up this session, but I will content myself with saying that government party members are the ones who are responsible for our not making better headway at this time. In these critical days our first thoughts should be with the gallant young men and young women, and their dependents, who are doing so much for us to-day.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I happen to speak at this stage of the debate, it is not, Mr. Speaker, because I want to be labelled as leader of any group, and on this point I should like to tranquillize the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) who, on February 1, in the course of the debate on the speech from the throne, mentioned the fact that he was speaking after many leaders, some of them, he said, leaders of "one man" parties. As I had been speaking before him, there is no doubt that his remarks were directed to me as well as to others who had spoken before him.
I believe the hon. member for Trinity is an able lawyer, and he must be aware of the fact that there can exist some independent members who do not need blindly to follow a leader, being able to think for themselves.
I happen to be here as representative of constituents who sent me to this house to represent their personal views and not the ideas of a party.
Since the beginning of this session we have discussed many projects relating to social security. Every group, and I should say every hon. member of this chamber, has had an opportunity of expressing his personal views on the different post-war projects, many of which have been discussed at great length. This goes to prove that everybody is anxious to look forward, and endeavour to prepare to his utmost capacity the future of our country.
There is no doubt that this sentiment is shared by the whole population, and especially by those who, at the present time, are engaged in the gigantic struggle, of which, thank God, we hope to see the end before long.
I should like to draw attention to the fact that, for the last few years, and especially during this session, many declarations made by persons in authority have led us to believe that this country is moving more and more toward greater centralization. All the new projects brought before the house for the purpose of social security bear in themselves this very danger of a greater centralization.
We must not set aside and we must never forget the basic principle which is the foundation of our national life and by which this parliament is bound to give its fullest respect to the constitution under which we live. We must never forget that the provinces constituting the Canadian federation also have their rights under our constitution, and my contention is that none of these new projects can produce good results if the provinces do not share the burden. The provinces should be called upon to collaborate with the dominion government, but should never be called to give up their own rights. If we refer to some declarations, we come to the conclusion that this government wants more than a collaboration on the part of the provinces.
From the discussions that took place on bill No. 82, for the establishment of a new Department of Reconstruction, I should like to quote a few sentences, which will show that I am right in scenting the danger which I have just mentioned. On June 20, in the course of the debate just mentioned, I find at page 4009 of Hansard the following words:
Mr. Gillis: They are always prepared to do it, but they always throw up a straw' man so that we cannot get through it, with the cooperation of the provinces. You hide behind the British North America Act.
The answer given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was as follows:
I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but he has referred to New Zealand. I wonder if he has brought out the point that they have only one government in New Zealand, a unitary government, which is able to do things. If there v-ere only one government in Canada, the lower age of sixty-five would now be in force.
Later on, in the same debate, at page 4013 of Hansard, I quote from the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Martin):
But this government has not overlooked the desirability of taking unto itself powers that now reside elsewhere. It attempted that in 1941, the first real attempt ever made in this country, by having a conference with the prov-
The Budget-Mr. Dorion

inces in this very chamber, to try to bring about some of the recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois report, with the idea of stream-lining, if you like, our legislative machinery, with the idea of rendering our legislative powers more efficient. Then, not having succeeded in that conference, it is now proceeding to another; and as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said to-day, steps and preparations are now under way for the holding of another conference between the dominion and the provinces.
I am afraid that such declarations constitute the best encouragement to the very few people who seem sometimes to favour a movement of separatism in our country.
I wish to state, however, that the parliamentary assistant to the Prime Minister on the same occasion expressed some views which are worthy of mention, and I should like to regard them as the guiding declarations of the next interprovincial conference. I quote from page 4062 of Hansard:
I think it must be evident from the attitude taken so far by the dominion and the members of the government that the conference will not be entered into with any thought of endeavouring merely to secure the transfer of constitutional and financial power by one side or the other. The conference aims to see what is best for the people of Canada, how their needs can be met and who can best meet them; and if, as I expect, the provinces meet the dominion in that spirit, we can look forward to a satisfactory arrangement to deal with all these questions.
These last words are worthy of mention, and they should be inserted in the agenda of the proposed conference.
Mention has been made quite a few times by the Prime Minister and others during this session that this interprovincial conference would be called soon. This conference Was announced by the Prime Minister in the very beginning of the session, and a few days ago he repeated his announcement and told the house that this conference would be held in a month or so.
There is no doubt that the people of this country have the right to ask if the purpose of this interprovincial conference will be the adoption of the Rowell-Sirois report which was shelved in 1941, when the premiers of the nine provinces met in Ottawa. If the purpose of the government is such, I contend that it should be well specified, so that the representatives of the provinces will know exactly what they are called for, and beforehand they can secure from their respective constituents their desires and yearnings.
I do not see any need for central government to infringe upon provincial rights to pass legislation even in matters of social security.
We have a very good experience of successful legislation in which the provincial and central governments collaborate; I mean the old age pension and other similar legislation.
[Mr. Dorion.)
The matter of provincial autonomy is very serious and should be dealt with extremely carefully.
Ever since confederation there has been a gradual and continuous movement for centralization of authority in the federal parliament. Many have been the conflicts between the federal and provincial governments in respect of jurisdiction.
We have to admit that the provinces are the real historic units around which centres all the glory of our history, the remembrance of early settlement and adversity', and the affection that clings to the family. The provinces, in the immediate sense, lie nearer to the hearts of most of our people than does the larger but more abstract conception of the dominion. This is all the more true, inasmuch as the provinces of Canada, if we take the prairies as one, represent actual units of history and physical units of geography. Hence the whole setting and background of our Canadian provinces seems to indicate them as the proper form of our natural life, separate groups of people each doing things in their own way and letting the others do the fame.
The case for provincial autonomy is made still stronger when we remember that one province, the oldest and the largest, Quebec, is for its French-Canadian people almost everything; and for some of them quite everything. It is almost all that history has left them of a regime that was their own, of the language and religion of their mother country.
In an article published in the Financial Post of January 8, 1944, written by Stephen Leacock, I read this:
The province of Quebec, wrote Andrew Macphail, is the last refuge of common sense in North America. We contrasted, . too, the tyranny of the Ontario Sunday, with the wholesome outdoor Sunday of the priests and their seminary scholars playing games together. We admire that quiet contentedness of the French-Canadian habitant and its contrast to the eager haste, the get-rich-quick, the quest-for-money of the restless English. We liked the stories that Doctor Drummond told us of Jean-Baptiste coming home' again from the States, of Louis Hemon's far-away and long-ago picture of the world of Marie Ohapdelaine. Around French Canada hung all the romance of history, and the respect for a people happy in their own lot. Above this level of the plain life of simple people was the pride felt by the educated and academic classes of society, living in a dual culture, in drawing upon two languages and two great literatures, on the traditions of two great nations.
This picture is true for the whole province of Quebec, and more particularly for the constituency which I have the honour to represent.

The Budget-Mr. Dorion
In the course of my trips across this vast area of over 300,000 square miles, it has been a great pleasure for me to meet citizens of all groups and all classes, and1 I must say, without fear of contradiction, that the people living in Charlevoix-Saguenay are most faithful, loyal and honest. They love their country; they love the soil from which they draw their living; they love the small piece of land where they raise their large families, praying the Almighty to be preserved from the evils that are spreading all over the world.
They are glad to collaborate with their fellow-citizens and give their contribution toward making this country as beautiful as possible, and a place where one can live happily; but they, in turn, need the collaboration of the governments, and the greatest of these needs consists in the establishment of better means of communication.
I have already said, and I will repeat it as long as the authorities refuse to hear my appeal, that the only means of developing this vast section of our country would be the construction of a road along the north shore of the St. Lawrence. We have seen in the war appropriations that this government is spend- . ring vast sums to build some roads in the western part of the country, and I am eager to see the day when the government will look up to the eastern part as well.
I said that our people live quietly and happily. I stated that they want to collaborate with their fellow-citizens, but they do not want to be replaced by foreigners of all descriptions. That is the reason why they are opposed to opening wide the doors of our country to facilitate immigration. On this question, I already had the opportunity on June 5 to say a few words in this house, and I should like to complete my remarks. Since this question of immigration will, no doubt, be one of the most important in the post-war period, I hope it will be discussed in every quarter with the broadest-minded spirit.
We very often hear some figures mentioned about the possibilities for Canada to absorb many million immigrants after the war. While listening to such declarations, I have always wondered if they were made in good faith, and if those who made them knew exactly what they were speaking about. One of the many reasons advanced for accepting immigrants in Canada is the contention that so many million immigrants will become so many million consumers; but I never heard that such figures were based on serious inquiries, and my first yioint is that the government, before allowing these immigrants to enter Canada, should make a complete survey throughout the *country to ascertain whether there is enough
space to absorb such immigrants. I challenge anyone to deny the necessity of such a survey being made with the least possible delay. Doubtless, we cannot compare our density of population in Canada with that of any other country, and I think it is stupid to contend that Canada is able to receive so many million immigrants on account of her vast area. The contentions that are based upon this comparison of areas are not serious ones and are made by those who ignore, as I already said, what they are talking about. In fact, everybody knows that in our country there is only a strip of land habitable, so that we easily come to the conclusion that available space throughout Canada is more limited than it is claimed to be in some quarters. The logical attitude to take would be not to accept immigrants before ascertaining that we need them, and before making a judicious choice of them.
I think nearly everybody in this country is willing to have new citizens come from abroad, but they also expect these newcomers to collaborate in building up a greater country, and that they will not be a burden for Canadian citizens.
Since we may not be afforded the time to discuss at full length the problem of immigration when the; civil estimates of the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) come before the house, I take advantage of this opportunity to express my views on this policy. I wish to state that it would be much better for us to keep Canadian-born citizens in Canada, rather than replacing them with newcomers. I am mentioning this, because if we refer to the "Canada Year Book" of 1942, we, see at page 91 a complete summary of the movement of the Canadian population for the last twenty years. 'It is entitled:
Summary of births, deaths, natural increase and immigration, calendar years, with estimated population as at June 1, 1921-40.
On June, 1, 1921, the population of Canada was 8,788,000. From 1921, to June 1, 1940, 797,036 immigrants came to Canada; in the same period of time, we had 2,432,609 births. Therefore, had we kept our newly-born Canadians together with the immigrants who came to Canada, our population should have increased to 12,017,645. According to the summary just mentioned, we see that on June 1, 1940, our population was 11,422,000; that is to say, about 600,000 less than we should have had. As mentioned, we received 797,000 immigrants and we lost 600,000 Canadian citizens. Have I not'the right to ask, where is the benefit in spending such large amounts of money for immigration when we cannot save our own citizens? To explain these figures, I must say that the ones which I have just read about newly-born Canadians are given after having
The Budget-Mr. Dorion

deducted the number of deaths. Is it not right to say that our money would be much better spent for the safe-keeping of our own citizens? I remember that, in previous years, a Canadian citizen from the province of Quebec who went to establish himself out west, had to pay more than immigrants coming from central Europe to the same place.
I said that this question of immigration was a very important one, and I base my contention on the report of the Department of Mines and Resources for the year ending. March, 1943. At page 175 of this report, I read the following sentences under the title, "Post-War Immigration". I quote:
Many suggestions are being received as to post-war immigration. These are being carefully examined and filed for future reference. It is everywhere recognized that Canada must, first of all, deal with the reestablishment of her own service personnel and their dependents and during that period turn the Canadian war industry to peace-time pursuits. The magnitude of this task cannot be known until the war is over.
Those best able to form an opinion agree that tens of thousands of the war-oppressed people of Europe will look to the western world for new homes when war has ceased. Few of these are likely to have funds either for transportation or settlement and many may require to be built up physically before being fit for transfer from Europe. How many and what type of settlers, especially those without capital, will Canada be able to absorb with benefit to the newcomers and to the dominion. Will the assistance given by the allies to the suffering millions of Europe after the war include financial assistance for migration and settlement?
We are fighting the most terrible war the world has ever known. We have spent millions and billions of money. Our young men have given their health and even their lives and all these sacrifices to prevent the invasion of our country and to epable our citizens to enjoy an enduring peace. I wonder if these tens of thousands of people of Europe, as mentioned in the quotation I just made, will not constitute what I would call a "pacific invasion" of our country with the possibility of the same result as if the invasion proper had taken place? Are we to allow all kinds of people to enter into Canada and let them spread among our population the ideologies and doctrines that lie at the base of the present war in Europe? I am amazed to see in an official report of this government a statement like the one which is included in the quotation I first read and which is as follows: How many and what type of settlers, especially those without capital, will Canada be able to absorb with benefit to the new-comers and to the dominion?
Is it not ridiculous to permit the entry into Canada of immigrants who will not even

be able to pay their own transportation and who will be nothing but a burden for our people?
Another very important aspect of the same question comes from a declaration made by the Prime Minister, on May 22, after his return from England, and I quote from pages 3099 and 3100 of Hansard:
I should like to add a further word as a result of what I have heard and seen and felt. I do not believe that this war is going to end the conflict between the different classes and races of men. The enemy of to-day must be completely destroyed, but forces of evil have been let loose in this world which it is going to be difficult indeed to bring to bay. These forces of evil are going to continue to destroy all that is best for mankind, I am fraid, for many days, possibly years, after the main struggle is over. In all our deliberations here, as I am sure will be the case in the deliberations of all other assemblies of free nations, we must never lose sight of the fact that our greatest work may still lie ahead in seeking to trample under foot and slay the dragon that to-day is seeking to destroy humanity itself.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister has said too much and too little. As far as I am concerned, I should have liked to learn from the Prime Minister what are the forces of evil to which he referred? They must consist of something untold; they must emanate from somewhere other than from our enemy territories, because otherwise they would be destroyed as our enemies will be, and we would not have to fear those evils, once the war is won. These forces of evil must be threatening from outside Canada, since every precaution has been taken to overcome subversive elements in Canada.
Therefore we must believe, first, that those forces of evil actually exist, since the Prime Minister mentioned them.
Second, they must come from outside, because otherwise our government would not be fulfilling its duty by allowing any subversive movement to flourish in our midst.
Third, they cannot be found in enemy territories, since the Prime Minister stated that they will continue to destroy all that is best for mankind even after the defeat of our enemies. Where do they come from? How could they penetrate our country, and what would be the best way to defend ourselves against such forces of evil?
Is it not true that the surest way to spare our country from these forces of evil, since they likely come from outside, would be caution in the selection of immigrants to enter Canada, because this would apparently be the means through which these forces could be brought in. Is it only by a sane immigration policy that Canada could be spared from them? Up to now, I believe that our government has

The Budget-Mr. Dorion
been much too lenient toward the so-called refugee, this problem being so closely connected with immigration.
In the "Canada Year Book" of 1942, under the title, "Immigration and Colonization-Refugee Immigration," we read subsection 8, as follows:
The term "refugee" in recent years, has *acquired a much wider application than when it became a familiar word after the first world war. Then it was applied mainly to those who had lost both homes and citizenship; latterly, it has been applied to all who, because of political, religious, racial or economic troubles, actual or threatened, have been forced or induced to move.
And further, at page 166, we read this:
For many years, the exodus of settlers was discouraged by emigration countries, but latterly the emigration of unwanted minorities has been encouraged although an increased effort has been made to retain their capital.
We must conclude that to the problem of immigration has been added the problem of refugees, and I wish to draw the attention of the government to the fact that under the War Measures Act the entry of refugees does not seem to have been dealt with accurately. I am of the opinion that we should have been, and should still be, more cautious with regard to this refugee immigration. It is always commendable to extend a helpful hand to ill-fortuned people who were crushed by dictators of conquered countries; but one must not forget that-Charity begins at home-and I can hardly conceive this virtue of charity practised to the extent of allowing all kinds of people to establish their homes in our midst without, prior to their coming, ascertaining that they are desirable subjects.
One wonders why the government deemed it advisable to cast aside the immigration law, as was the case recently. I wish to state first that in our immigration law, chapter 93 of the revised statutes, we find the necessary protection against the intrusion of undesirable elements. Section 4 provides that the minister may issue a written permit authorizing any person to enter Canada, to remain therein, without being subject to the provisions of this act. In accordance with this provision of the law, at the beginning of the present session the Minister of Mines and Resources tabled sessional paper 46 on Friday, January 28. In this document we see that only two special permits were issued during the calendar year 1943 to the two persons mentioned in the said document. I wonder why all the permits issued by the same department to many hundred refugees have not been issued under the same section.
In fact an order in council was passed on the 10th December, 1943. That order, P.C. 9440, in part reads as follows:
Section 1. Notwithstanding any provision of the Immigration Act, chapter 93 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, or any amendment thereto, or of order in council P.C. 2653 of September 14, 1939, the Minister of Mines and Resources or any person thereunto authorized by him may issue a temporary permit to enter Canada to any refugee transferred to Canada from the United Kingdom whose release in Canada has been approved by the appropriate authorities.
Paragraph (c) of section 2 reads:
(c) be subject to the provisions of the national selective' service (civilian) regulations in the same manner and to the same extent as any other person in Canada.
It appears by this last paragraph that these refugees can have the benefit of the national selective service regulations but are not subject to the military call-up. There is another reason why one wonders why we did not apply the immigration law, and this wondering derives from the fact that in the order in council just mentioned it is explicitly stated that chapter 93 of the revised statutes does not apply. If we look at section 3 of chapter 93 we see provisions for the protection of our people, as well as our institutions, which are expressly set aside by the P.C. 9440. In this section appears a list of prohibited classes, and it is worth mentioning some of them. They are as follows:
Idiots and imbeciles	Spies
Deaf and dumb	Criminals
Prostitutes	Alcoholics
Vagrants	Revolutionaries
Invalids	Traitors
And especially those mentioned in paragraph (n) of the said section 3, that is to Bay:
Persons who believe in or advocate the overthrow by force or violence of the government of Canada or of constituted law and authority, or who disbelieve in or are opposed to organized government, or who advocate the assassination of public officials, or who advocate or teach the unlawful destruction of property.
After having taken cognizance of the above-mentioned order in council, I thought it advisable to inquire about the number of refugees who had been admitted to Canada by virtue of this order. On January 26, I asked some questions on the orders of the day, and one of them read as follows:
How many permits have been issued by the Minister of Mines and Resources, or by any person authorized by him, under order in council P.C. 9440, December 10, 1943?
The answer given by the minister was: "932." Wishing to know who these refugees were, I subsequently asked another question to find out the names, previous residence and racial origin
The Budget-Mr. Dorion

of the persons to whom these permits had been issued. In answer to my question, sessional paper 48-A was tabled on April 17. It showed that more than ninety per cent of these permits had been issued to Hebrews.
I wish to state here most emphatically that at all times I am ready to comply with the directions given by the Roman Catholic church, and to consider the Hebrews as any other people. I have nothing against them. During my twenty-three years of law practice in Quebec, I have had occasion to deal with them quite often, and I do not hesitate to say that they must be considered on the same footing as any other people; but my contention is that they must not enjoy any special privileges and I will endeavour to show that, since the beginning of the present war on too many occasions we have seen special privileges extended to them; so much so that, at times, we are wondering whether or not we were engaged' in this war for the sole purpose of saving or helping out the Jews all over the world. Here in Canada our attention has been drawn very often, to all kinds of organizations to help the ill-fated Jews. As an example, an association was formed some time ago, under the name of "United Jewish Refugees and War Relief Agencies," with its head office at 1121 St. Catherine street west Montreal. They also have branches in Toronto and Winnipeg, under the chairmanship of Samuel Bronfman.
Under the auspices of this association a campaign was launched throughout Canada, sponsored by Senator Cairine R. Wilson, chairman of the national committee on refugees. The purpose of this campaign was to gather some 500,000 signatures in support of a petition to the Canadian government. I hold in my hand a copy of this petition in which they asked the government of Canada: I quote:
1.	To offer the sanctuary of Canada to refugees from political or religious persecution without regard, to race, creed or financial condition.
2.	To take immediate steps to facilitate the entry into Canada of refugees (especially those stranded in Portugal) whom it is possible to rescue.
3.	To make any changes in the Immigration Act, regulations or administration thereof necessary to admit such refugees into Canada.
I do not know whether this petition ever reached the government, but I am aware that in order to encourage this movement a Canadian immigration office was opened at Lisbon, Portugal, in October, 1943, for the purpose of examining refugees applying for sanctuary in Canada and for granting appropriate visas. Later on, the house was informed that a few

hundred refugees were coming into Canada each month under this new scheme.
Must I come to the conclusion that these petitions had a much better result than some other petitions that were presented to the Prime Minister by Canadian citizens and municipal corporations? On March 27 I asked the Prime Minister, as recorded at page 1861 of Hansard:
How many municipal corporations and public bodies have forwarded to the Prime Minister resolutions requesting the full application of the provisions of the Immigration Act with regard to any individual who wishes to enter this country ?
This is what the Prime Minister answered:
Mr. Speaker, I am informed that there have been forwarded to my office a large number of resolutions on the subject referred to. The resolutions are similarly worded. It is perfectly evident some one or more persons have been circulating communications with a view to having them forwarded to my office. The question is of the kind which, rvere it to be answered literally, might convey a wholly erroneous impression. For example, I might say I have received thousands of communications identically worded concerning some things-the postage being free. Were I asked to recall how many of these have been received, and were to say that thousands had come in, such an answer would be wholly misleading. For the most part they would represent the opinions of a mere handful of persons. There have not been thousands in this case, but an answer as to the number that have come in would be misleading the public as to the significance of the reply given. I think therefore that the question should not be answered.
Having personally received some duplicates of these resolutions, I know they were passed legally and regularly at a meeting of each municipal corporation which had adopted them, and I really was amazed to notice how little concerned was the Prime Minister about these resolutions. Must we come to the conclusion that the Jewish refugees deserve much better attention from our government than our Canadiamborn citizens?
At this stage of my remarks I should like to make a suggestion; I would not say for the solution of this very difficult problem, but at least as an attempt to bring about a solution. I believe that the Canadian government should follow the rulings of the British North America Act on this question, which we find at section 95 of the act which reads as follows:
In each province, the legislature may make laws in relation to agriculture in the province, and to immigration into the province; and it is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may, from time to time, make laws in relation to agriculture in all or any of the provinces, and to immigration into all or any of the provinces; and any law of the legislature of a province relative to agriculture or to immigration shall have effect in and for the province as long as it is not repugnant to any act of the parliament of Canada.

The Budget-Mr. McGarry
This section, was in accordance with the Quebec resolutions of 1864 and the London resolutions of 1866.
I have always believed that in all our internal policies, if we followed as closely as possible the terms of the British North America Act, we would not be so often faced with so many difficulties as have been encountered more in recent years than ever before.
On this question of immigration there is no doubt that the provincial governments are much more aware of the needs and possibilities of their respective provinces. They are in closer relation with the people, with the municipal bodies, and are in a much better position to determine what kind of immigration they should allow in order that their economic life, as well as their social and political life, - may not be interfered with and so that the efforts of the people to make this country the ideal place to live in may not be hampered.
In conclusion I would suggest that this government request the provincial governments to pass legislation, and, in this way, to make known their views on the matter. I suggest that this section 95 of the British North America Act has been too much overlooked in the past and that, after the present war, it will be more essential than ever before to have it put into application.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again that hardy
annual, the budget, has made its appearance in the house. I think all would admit that it received a most lucid and eloquent interpretation at the hands of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley). I also feel assured that it had a very good reception at least from a majority of members in the house and from the public generally.
It will be noticed that it has not diminished very much in stature, since it made its last appearance. After all, I do not think that is contrary to the anticipation of hon. members or the public in general. It will be remembered that this is primarily a war-time budget and, although we have now experienced almost six years of this reign of death and destruction, it is quite evident that that tragedy of carnage has not yet ceased, and no one can forecast when the end will come.
Moreover, it would appear that we would be wise in anticipating that, from now until the end, this conflict will become more intensive in character than has been experienced in the war up to now. Therefore it is wise on the part of the government to provide proper financial arrangements, and wise for us who are
interested in the war to be prepared to exercise every ounce of faith, enthusiasm, energy and strength within our power. It behooves us now to be prepared to put forth an even greater war effort than we hitherto have done.
I shall not tire the house by entering into a detailed recitation of the achievements of this dominion in its war effort, nor shall I set out what it has done in both economic and military fields of endeavour. I believe it would be sufficient to say that it has received the plaudits of the whole of the Canadian people, and that it has received the praise and admiration of our allies, and has merited praise from every worth-while journal on the north American continent. In fact, so wise has been our economic policy to maintain the strain of war and to prevent deflation after the war is over, that, in large measure, our economic policy wras copied by the great nation to the south of us.
It was pointed out in the speech from the throne that the government had primarly in mind the successful prosecution of the war, and I think it will be accepted by the unprejudiced mind that it has adhered fairly closely to that policy. When we realize the cooperation the government has received from every element of our citizenship-from labour, industry, the farmers, the fishermen and the merchant marine-it appears quite clear that the nation as a whole has become conscious of the importance of putting forth our very 'best efforts in order to defeat the challenge of those who would dominate the world.
References also were made in the speech from the throne to other measures regarded as essential to deal with our post-war problems. There was reference in the speech from the throne to measures which would be introduced, debated and put on the statute books in order to deal with our post-war problems. These are classified as measures of rehabilitation and reconstruction, and I think all will agree that they are timely. I believe the government w7as wise, first of all to anticipate those problems, and then to introduce measures to deal with them. I think we owe that to our fighting men, the men who have experienced the hardships and the horrors of war. It behooves us to show these men when they return to their homeland that they will have security, and will live in a democracy worthy of the blood, sweat and tears they have expended in its behalf.
While I admit that the prosecution of the war should be foremost in the thoughts and intent of our people, yet I consider that the government is only showing wisdom when it has some regard and does some planning for
The Budget-Mr. McGarry

possibly 2,000,000 of our citizens who are now engaged in industry and are on active service, and who will return to the land or revert to their ordinary pursuits in life. I think every unprejudiced person will admit that from the inception of this war the government has attempted to prepare plans and schemes to deal with our post-war problems. Three hours after war was declared, the government established the wartime prices and trade board. Every one knows the beneficial effects of this action. During the war there has been no hoarding or no unnecessary scarcities. We have not had the disgraceful spectacle we had in the last war where certain men and corporations waxed rich on the sacrifices and blood of the nation. This was a great and cautious measure undertaken by the government immediately after the beginning of the war.
We come next to soldier reestablishment. We all remember the old Soldier Settlement Act which did not prove very satisfactory. Throughout my constituency, and I believe on the island of Cape Breton generally, it was characterized as a racket. Apparently no precautions were taken to afford security to the settler. In many cases men with no farming experience were placed on unproductive farms. With the two main essentials for success lacking, the result was that in one or two years many of these farms were vacated. Not only have the new amendments improved the act of the last war, but its provisions have been extended.
To-day men are placed on farms under certain regulations. First of all the farm must be sufficiently productive to support a man and his family and, next, the man must have some knowledge of farming. If he has not that knowledge he is given an opportunity to prepare himself to work on a farm and make a substantial living. The same rights and privileges are extended to men who work in small industries and to fishermen, men who can devote only part of their time to agricultural pursuits. They will receive the same concessions granted to those 'who can devote themselves entirely to agriculture.
Then there is the compulsory employment act which was passed by this government during the war. This will be of some help in solving our post-war problems. When a man leaves employment to enlist for active service he has the right to claim that employment upon his return.
Then there is the Unemployment Insurance Act. No one will say that that is not a provision to deal with the unemployment problem which is sure to show its ugly head after this war. The introduction of that act was quite timely because it was brought in
IMr. McGarry.]
when there was no unemployment. The result is that to-day we have a repository of money which will provide much of the finances needed to help, at least temporarily, in solving any unemployment conditions.
We come next to the matter of reconstruction and rehabilitation. These matters have been under study for the last two years by a committee of this house. The knowledge obtained from experts who have been before the committee is certainly worth while. I trust that when the provisions of this scheme are put into operation they will be dominionwide and that special care will be given to those parts of Canada where the need for rehabilitation and reconstruction is more strongly indicated.
At the risk of being accused of being too regional, I consider that Nova Scotia, Cape Breton island and the constituency I have the honour to represent in particular will be the first parts of Canada to receive a practical application of this rehabilitation scheme. There is no part of this dominion which has received less support of that kind. On Cape Breton island and in the constituency which I represent we have many resources, on the land, in the forest and in the sea. Wrapped up in the rocks and in the bowels of the earth is enough mineral wealth to make us all happy and rich. In addition, Cape Breton island is a veritable tourist mecca. If our economic condition is below par it is not because of a lack of resources; it is not because of a lack of brain and brawn; it is owing to the fact that in spite of the industry and intelligence of our people there remain problems which they themselves cannot solve without governmental assistance.
One of our greatest problems is that of transportation, and a large part of this problem is caused by the bottleneck which exists between the great city of Sydney and the mainland of Nova Scotia. Our transportation condition is such that at the present time a locomotive can haul only eighteen cars from Sydney to Point Tupper, but the same locomotive can haul eighty loaded cars from Moncton west. This haulage inadequacy, if I may so term it, is because of a very high grade and many curves on the road.
That is not the only trouble. Not only are we suffering from a lack of haulage facilities, but we are subjected to a delay of from five to seven hours on account of having to ferry our freight and our passengers across the strait of Canso. In other words, a loaded train arriving at Point Tupper which has to be ferried to Mulgrave will reach Truro seven

The Budget-Mr. McGarry
hours later than it would if the train could cross a bridge or causeway. It costs $500,000 to operate the car ferries at Point Tupper, to say nothing of the capital replacement after a certain number of years. There is operating across that strait a highway, now operating at a loss. If a causeway were built there it would afford a passage for cars, and that project which to-day is operating at a loss would become a source of revenue simply through a toll being charged for crossing the bridge. The people of Cape Breton are vitally concerned in this matter. There is very much ado about the cost of this project; but we, in Cape Breton, realize that we have been contributing to projects in other parts of Canada from which we derive no physical or financial benefit, and when we consider what has been expended in that way we feel justified in saying that the matter of cost should not enter into this scheme at all. The first and only consideration should be to supply proper transportation so as to overcome the inadequacy from which we are suffering. It is pretty nearly time that the people of Canada when they are speaking of the eastern and western boundaries of this great dominion of ours should say, "from Sydney to Vancouver", instead of saying from "Halifax to Vancouver". I think this project is economically sound. It would be costly, no doubt, but it is certainly a project to which our people are entitled.
That is not all I have to say about transportation facilities in our part of the country. In my constituency there are two short lines of railroads. We have a railroad from Point Tupper to St. Peters in Richmond county. We have another railroad from Point Tupper to Inverness in Inverness county. Both of these roads should be further extended. The development which has taken place in the fishing, lumbering and farming industries north of Inverness warrants the extension of that railway in order to provide proper and adequate transportation facilities for that section of the country. There is another reason why this extension should be made. From the town oi Inverness to Margaree harbour is a belt ol coal which has lain undeveloped, I believe just for lack of the transportation facilities which this extension would provide.
I should like to add this further word about our transportation facilities. The train from Point Tupper to Inverness as well as the train from Point Tupper to St. Peters consists of one passenger coach and a number of freight cars. If you want to have a good example of one of the relics of olden times you should take a ride on the coach of each of these trains. The heating system is terrible. It is so bad that it renders the coach air-polluted rather
than air-conditioned. The only compensating thing about it is that the coal gas renders the passengers, if they have any distance to go, sort of semi-conscious, so that they do not feel the bumps from the uncomfortable seats in that coach. I would suggest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Michaud) that he substitute for this air-polluted mobile contraption-I cannot call it anything else-a fairly decent passenger coach that would not tax the respiratory organs of the passengers and would not be so severe on their dorsalis and gluteus maximus muscles. I think that is something which our people deserve. We have been tolerant. We know the conditions of war; we know the scarcity of materials; nevertheless we feel that just so soon as it is possible to make this substitution it should be done.
Another thing that should be given careful consideration in the rehabilitation programme is our fisheries. We have in the north of Inverness county three large cooperative fisheries, and we have three private individuals who are carrying on that industry there in a big way. But under the circumstances, with a lack of facilities, they are not able to reach anything like maximum production or get the price which they should for their fish. We all know that the marketing of fish to-day has changed materially from conditions prevailing a few years back. You can no longer tie a rope about a cantle of fish and ship it and sell it on the market. Mackerel to-day must be filleted. You cannot put it on the market round. The best codfish to-day is processed into boneless fish. These products are perishable, and there are no refrigeration facilities. They cannot be processed profitably because of the lack of refrigeration facilities. Local refrigeration is a necessity in carrying on this work. I have been trying for the last three or four years to get a refrigeration plant in the centre of the north at Grand Etang. When one looks around and sees all that these people have done under the greatest handicaps I certainly cannot understand why we should not at least encourage them in the wonderful efforts they have already made by providing them with refrigeration facilities.
At Cheticamp a few years ago we had a life-saving boat. This possibly does not seem to hon. gentlemen a very important thing, but I can tell this house and the minister that the lack of that life-saving boat at Cheticamp is responsible for a lack of production of fish. I will tell you why. The men are operating in that section with small boats and they are not going to attempt to go any distance outside where probably the fish a're schooling unless the weather is quite evidently fine. If there

The Budget-Mr. McGarry

is any suspicion or forecast of bad weather they refuse to go out; whereas, if they had a life-saving boat at Cheticamp, they would feel that if they got into trouble there would be some refuge in the storm. I urge upon the minister the consideration of this very important matter. It would not be costly, because it would mean only a few hundred dollars, and I can assure him that it would have a great effect on the production of fish in that area.
Lumbering is another thing that will receive consideration under the rehabilitation scheme. The lumber industry in my constituency is one of our greatest industries. The province of Nova Scotia has done a great deal in the way of conserving our forests and in encouraging that industry in many ways. From the revenue that is accruing to the dominion from that industry, I really think something more should be done to encourage it.
What I have said about fisheries in the county of Inverness applies also to the counties of Richmond and West Cape Breton. These people, alone and unaided, have done wonderful work in that industry. They have established cooperatives there, and they are carrying on, under difficulties, a business which is very important not only to themselves but to the dominion as a whole.
Another thing that should come under the rehabilitation scheme is an intensive geological survey of our mineral wealth. I believe that if any section of this dominion has been almost absolutely immune from research of this kind it is the island of Cape Breton, and I would urge upon the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) that he see to it that as a postwar programme, and knitted into the fabric of rehabilitation, there should be an intensive research into our minerals, which I believe exist in abundance although they have not yet been -revealed.
Another industry that will receive consideration, and one that should be considered particularly in my constituency, is the farming industry. As has already been pointed out to the house, there are hundreds of thousands of fertile acres in Nova Scotia which are submerged, and each year these submerged areas are increasing. This does not mean that our farmers are negligent or that they are not trying to help themselves; but this is a problem in which they cannot help themselves, and this reclamation of land, and the preservation of other land that will be overrun if some precaution is not taken, is one of the most important things I can conceive of in the province from which I come.
Talking about centralization and decentralization, another thing we are suffering from

in the island of Cape Breton, is the lack of an abattoir. The result is that our people in Cape Breton during this war have not been allowed the bonus on hogs simply because the only abattoir to which we have access is in Moncton, New Brunswick, and the cost of transporting our live stock there is too great. Moreover, the inconvenience is quite a serious matter. I think we should have an abattoir on the island of Cape Breton.
Something else which I believe is indicated is some sort of experimental station, a farm owned by the government, for the purpose of encouraging our people in the industry, setting an example in the way of increasing our stock and improving it, and interesting our people in sheep raising or something of that sort, for which our country is well adapted. I know several sites in my constituency which would be very suitable for an experimental farm of that kind, not far removed from a market, with splendid water, enough acreage, good pasturage, and surrounded by the most prominent farmers in the constituency.
We have heard something about the civil aviation scheme. I hope, when that is put into effect, our section of the country will not be overlooked. We have one of the most suitable sites for an airport right on !he very brim of Cape Breton Highland park, and after this war, with our tourist meccas we have all around us, we expect that the influx of tourist traffic will mean to us the greatest revenue of all our industries.
We know also that these men who come to visit our country, in order to admire our scenic beauties and to bask in our restful surroundings, have not very much time to spare, and I do not doubt that many hundreds, yes, thousands, of these people will come to our meccas by plane. I said before, we have, adjoining our national park, one of the best sites in Nova Scotia for an air field. I would ask the minister, who is so greatly interested in the matter, when the house closes, if he is looking around for a place to admire beautiful scenery and to get a rest such as he would never obtain in any other part of the world, to look over our prospects in that direction.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the words that I have to direct to you to-night are words which I can assure you are not going to be concerned with my own particular constituency. I intend to speak in a broader sense. My remarks will apply to the whole Dominion of Canada, because in some way or another I feel that once a member is elected to the House of Commons he ceases to. be the representative of the small community in Canada from which he comes. He must take a larger perspective and try to improve the dominion as a whole. He should not particularly confine his efforts to one small locality in the dominion.
I wish to say a few words to-night on the budget which has just been brought down. All: hon. members recall that last year when the budget was brought down we were exceedingly shocked at the size of it, only because it was the biggest we ever had. We were not unduly concerned because we knew that a war was on and it had to be financed. We thought then that $5,360,000,000 was a lot of money, and it was. This year we have gone over that again, and have brought down the largest budget in: the history of Canada. In spite of that, we' are going to be able to carry on. There is no: question about that.
One of the things which is most noticeable in the budget is that there is, generally speaking, no change in it, in so far as principle is concerned, from any other budget that has been presented. The same principle of taxation and borrowing is being followed. I could not help being impressed when the minister was speaking. One of the things he emphasized was the fact that there was not to be any higher taxation. I am sure we were all pleased with that. But I often wonder how there could be any higher taxation, because we have reached the height of taxation now. We are taking everything from the people that they can possibly afford to give. We have taken everything that the market can stand. The' social credit conception would be that it is not necessary to place such tremendous taxation on the people, and yet we could finance the war just as efficiently as it has been. It has always been my contention that we could finance this war with less taxation, but not without some taxation. The taxation would not necessarily be as great as it is now.
I am not surprised at the lack of change in policy, because the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) is-and I am sure he will not mind my saying this-a determined old, orthodox financier. He follows the school of orthodox financing as has been done by every government that has been in power. I am sometimes amazed at the official opposition criticiz-
4376	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
ing the present government when I remember that their party were in power during the last war and they financed in exactly the same way. Why should they point a finger of criticism at this government? As far as I can remember they have never offered any suggestions to this government showing how they would finance differently. I see the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) shaking his head. I must make a correction there because the government has created a little national money. May I say to him that if it had not been for the teachings of the Social Credit party I fear they would not have gone as far in that direction as they have? In that respect may I congratulate the government because I think it was a worthwhile action. I am afraid we cannot expect from this government and certainly not from the Progressive Conservative party, when and if they get into power, any radical change in financial policy. Therefore we shall have to continue in peace as well as in war to finance in exactly the same way as we are now doing; that is, by taxation and borrowing, with the limited amount of nationally created currency that this government has issued. But I wonder how the (Minister of Finance and his advisers can possibly conceive of this system going on year after year, continually building up the tremendous debt that we are building up, with-[DOT]out some change in policy.
A year ago the national debt stood at :about eleven and a half billions of dollars. I have the figures here for this year. I think the increase was about two and three-quarter billions of dollars. That makes our national debt, funded and unfunded, about fourteen billion dollars. That is a tremendous load for the country to carry. It would not be so bad if that were to be the limit of the load. But the load is going to continue to pile up higher and higher, and as I see it we have not much prospect, despite the hopes and the pious platitudes of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the other day, of our debt decreasing after this war. Therefore we shall have to pay the tremendous interest charge which is a continuing yearly charge upon the people, and we shall have to tax the people for it. When We do that we lower their standard of living to that extent. It is a fixed charge and cannot be changed.
I know the minister has financed in part by the sale of victory bonds. I am not going to say a great deal about that other than that if a man has the money to invest in victory bonds, then I think it is a good business proposition because he gets a good return on his money. It permits him to put
(Mr. C. E. Johnston.]
money away for a rainy day or to use it after the war is over when there is no danger of inflation. To that extent I agree with the minister. But I fear that in too many cases there has been too much pressure put on the people to buy bonds, and then as soon as the victory bond sale is over and the people need that money-in some cases they had to go out and borrow the money to buy the bonds when they could ill afford to do it- they turn around and cash in on the bonds. That is so because the Minister of Finance must keep on cautioning the people against doing it. Every year he has cautioned them about the same thing, but when a man borrows money to buy a bond and cannot afford to pay it back, the only thing he can do is to cash the bond. However, I shall deal with that a little later on. The minister also mentioned the number of people who held victory bonds, while at the same time he was alarmed at the rate at which they were being cashed. He stated that about one-sixth of our people have bought victory bonds, which leaves about five-sixths of the people without bonds, but those five-sixths of the people are to be taxed in order to pay the interest on the bonds held by the other one-sixth.

It all comes back to the complaint we have made year after year, that the interest on our bonded indebtedness will be paid to a very few people, while the great majority of Canadians will have to be taxed to pay it. So that the vicious circle continues. In my opinion that is all quite unnecessary, but if the people persist in electing orthodox governments which are dead-set against reform, they will have to take the consequences. It will not make any difference whether they elect a Conservative or a Liberal administration; they will be saddled with the old, orthodox financial machine that will carry on just as it did in the past.
As I read over the budget speech of the minister I recalled the words of the Prime Minister in 1935 when he said, "If you elect me to head the government of Canada I will

I was pleased to see the government do one thing; that is, insititute family allowances. Now, for a few moments, I should like to refer to that part of the budget dealing with agriculture. I am very much afraid that agriculture has been overlooked once more. As yet I have been unable to discover any definite policy laid down for agriculture. I know that on several occasions the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has made much ado about how he was directing agriculture. One year he says that the farmers should raise large quantities of wheat. Another year he says not to raise so much wheat but to go into hogs. The next year he tells the farmers IMr. C. E. Johnston.]
And I have called attention to the date as being May 10.
-and we believe they should have the latest information regarding the wheat situation We also believe they should be frankly advised of the necessity of substantially increased wheat acreage this spring before it is too late. We had hoped that before this eleventh hour a definite statement with final advice would have been made either by the dominion Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Com-(TV5'e' The last statement on production for 1944 was made from Ottawa following the production conference held in Ottawa last December, and the farmer was advised not to increase wheat acreage The wheat situation has changed from one of large available supplies pressing heavily upon limited demand into a position where the wheat problem next year will be largely in terms of receiving and transporting enough wheat to supply the market.
Then he goes on to give the carryover in each of the years. I wish, however, to read a little more of the statement. And remember, this is the president of the wheat pool, a man who speaks with some authority. He declares, in regard to our production of wheat:
,	wheat glut is gone-our concern now
should be a possible shortage in supply in the event of a short crop or crop failure". He recommended^ to farmers as a sound policy for 1944 production:
1.	Make provision for necessary feed grain requirements with some surplus.
2.	Get back to normal summer-fallow acreage to fat sound farming practice on each farm.
In other words, he is repudiating entirely what the Minister of Agriculture has advocated, when he has been jumping from here to there. He is advising the farmers to go back to a regular method of farming, because they are the best judges. All we have to do is to indicate to them the amount we want, and they will arrange their plans so as to produce it. Then it continues:
3.	Sow every available acre to wheat with
