When you have things like that coming up year after year, is there any wonder that the farmers of this country-not only those in the west, but throughout the whole of Canada- find themselves in a great state of confusion?

The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
I am not going to say that the government has not done something for agriculture, but what it has done has come rather late. One of the great mistakes that has been made in the past has been that prices of agricultural commodities have not been fixed so that the farmer would get his cost of production, plus a fair profit. I am not one who advocates that any industry or any individual should work for nothing. I think the individual is entitled to a profit. If he happens to be an industrialist, then I say that he is entitled to his cost of production, plus a fair profit. If that is true of one industry, then necessarily it is true of another.
When the war began, agriculture suffered particularly. They started out with low prices for their commodities, but the wages they had to pay and the prices they had to pay for machinery jumped immediately-as is always the case. Therefore I say that agriculture has suffered, from the beginning of the war.
What was the excuse given then? I remember a speech that was printed in the newspapers, reporting what had been said by the Minister of Finance when speaking in Toronto. On that occasion he objected to the increase in prices of farm commodities, for fear that it would cause inflation. Well, wheat was only ninety cents a bushel at that time; since then it has been increased to $1.25-somewhere near where it should be-and there is no inflation. But despite the fact that the farmers are now receiving a fair price-and most people think it is a really good price whereas, as a matter of fact, it is not a good price, when one considers the high cost of wages and machinery and of living, and all those other things the farmer has to buy-they are not making much money. I shall prove that, in a moment or two.
I have before me a return affecting Alberta, and published by the agricultural extension service of the Department of Agriculture in that province. This was issued in January, 1944, and was published at the direction of the Hon. D. B. Macmillan, Minister of Agriculture of that province. I have looked through this statement, with considerable concern, because I had in mind a statement put on Hansard by the Minister of Agriculture showing how agriculture throughout the whole of Canada was so prosperous. On this sheet, under the heading of grain crops, including wheat, oats, barley, rye, peas, beans, mixed grains and flax seed, we End that the total value of those crops for 1942 was $214,753,000, whereas in 1943 it was *only $176,309,000, showing a decided drop. In the west, gram crops have always constituted
the greater part of the farmers' cash income.
In this instance, however, we find a drop of approximately $40,000,000.
I know the Minister of Agriculture would reply immediately, " Oh, well; they made up the difference in what they gained from their sale of live stock, including bacon and beef." Let us see what they did gain. Live stock, including horses, cattle, calves, sheep and lambs and hogs, were produced in 1942 to a value of $75,729,300, whereas in 1943 the value was $92,838,800, showing an increase of roughly $17,000,000. So that they did make a small increase there. But it will be noticed that they lost over $38,000,000 on their grain.
Let us see what the grand total is-and this is where we find out whether or not agriculture has prospered. The value of production of grain, root and fodder crops, animals slaughtered and sold, dairy produce, poultry produce, honey and wool in 1942 was $362,411,700, and in 1943 it had decreased to $347,280,900, showing a drop of $15,130,800.
Therefore it is certainly clear that agriculture is not making very much out of this war.
I am not saying that the farmers should make money out of the war; I do not think anybody should make anything out of it. But some people have the idea that agriculture is making tremendous money at $125 a bushel for wheat. Of coure that idea is exploded entirely. And, as I am reminded by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), the price of $1.25 has been operative only since last September. These figures will prove definitely that agriculture is not, in my estimation, getting what it should.
If we are to have agriculture as a basic industry in Canada-and I do not think we shall ever get away from that-then we must fix our future agricultural prices so that our farmers will be guaranteed, from the sale of their crops, a fair share of the national income. This may be difficult to figure out, but I think we can start on the basis accepted to-day. We can pay $1.25 for wheat, for example, along with the participation certificates. We could do the same in connection with cattle and hogs. Then, at the end of the year, after estimating the total revenue in that year, certificates could be issued to the farmers in amounts sufficient to make up their fair share of the national income.
Taking the average price during the period between 1915 and 1919, we find that that was the only period in which the fanner received his fair share of national income. I think that what I have suggested must be done. The only way that can be done is as we have expressed in a resolution which stands on the
The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)

order paper in my name. I am going to read this so that all may see just what we mean. It was presented on February 7 and it reads:
Whereas agriculture has seldom received its fair share of the national income of Canada;
And whereas the cost of producing all agricultural products varies considerably from year to year;
Therefore be it resolved,-That, in the opinion of this house and in the interest of the nation as a whole, the government he requested to set the prices of agricultural products at such a level that it will guarantee to the farmers of Canada such a yearly percentage of the national income as will have the same relation to the national income as the agricultural population bears to the national population of Canada.
That, in effect, is exactly the stand we thint-should be taken. Agriculture would then have no complaint because it would be getting its fair share of the national income.
There is another problem facing not only agriculture but other industries. I refer to man-power. This has a bearing upon agriculture, industry and the active army, and the problem is becoming more acute every day. It did not result overnight; it resulted in the first instance from lack of a sound policy on the part of the present government. The fact of the matter is that the government used neither skill nor foresight in the formation of its policy, but was guided almost entirely by political expediency and consideration.
Now that the invasion has started and our casualty lists grow, replacements become more urgent. The difficulty will certainly not be lessened. The government must accept their responsibility; they cannot side-step the issue. It must be faced. As time goes on, it will become more serious. I am not going to say anything more about the man-power policy, but a lot of difficulty lies ahead for agriculture,' industry and especially for the armed forces! I have spoken on the question before and I am not going to labour it to any great extent. However, for a minute I wish to refer to the labour problem and then I am through. I spoke on this on the speech from the throne and I do not want to cover ground covered already. I do not think the speech of the Minister of Finance delivered the other day is sound m logic, and I should like to quote briefly from his remarks as quoted in Hansard I quote first from page 4177 as follows:
I have been forced to the conclusion-
Forced, mind you!
that it would be a desirable change in o income tax law to discontinue the refundat feature of the income tax leaving as the fi rates of taxation, the rates of pure, no refundable tax as they now stand, and depen mg on voluntary savings to replace the pro?ee or the compulsory saving provision.

I cannot understand the logic of that. He wants to give relief by withdrawing the compulsory portion of the tax, and at the same time he wants the people to turn around and invest in bonds. Where will be the relief if they follow that advice? They will be short of money in any event. I believe the Minister of Finance was on sound ground when he had the compulsory savings. It was fair, and he so stated. To expect that that money will be put into victory bonds is not going to accomplish what he desires to accomplish. As he has pointed out, the people are continually cashing them in, which defeats his purpose. He goes on to say:
The refundable feature of our income tax law piovided simply a method of borrowing and of borrowing for progressively shorter terms as the war goes on. With the provision of allowances for contractual savings, it embodied a principle of fairness which I regret to relinquish.
Then why did he relinquish it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For the reasons stated in the speech.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There again I think the minister was unsound in his conclusion. As I read this over, I begin to think he did that against his better judgment. I may be wrong, but certainly I think he was wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I gave the reasons in my speech.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister said, "I have been forced to the conclusion". What that means is a matter of interpretation; nevertheless it is there. It seems to me that in that statement the minister was admitting that this was another thing which had been done because of political expediency. I hesitate to make a statement of that kind, but I am almost forced to do it. The minister continued:
Nevertheless, .if this particular method of borrowing, despite its virtues, has the one fault ot discouraging production at this critical period of the war, or if by its rigidity it creates hardship among those, income groups whose incomes leave little room for adjustment, then another method of borrowing must be found.
It is recommended, therefore, that no further deductions -for the refundable or savings portion be made after June 30, 1944.
He says that it discourages production; yet he is going to give back the refundable portion and ask the people to invest in bonds. They will be short just the same. That is not going to increase the amount of money they have. It will help them for the time being, but it will not relieve them of any burden of taxation. If the minister were sincere I think he

The Budget-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
should have left in the compulsory saving and freed from taxation all overtime which would provide the required increased production.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will speak about that later on. Has the hon. member really thought more than three minutes about it?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am just taking what the minister said. I do not think he has given a great deal of consideration to it himself because it is so confusing. I will not say anything further on that because he is going to add to the confusion at a later time, he says.
I wish to conclude my remarks by quoting a short paragraph which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, February 26, as a reprint from the Western Producer. I quote:
Whether we like it or not we shall be compelled to cross the boundaries erected by orthodox economists and politicians and to find and establish a method of distributing our products to our own people-a method which will not be affected by the volume of world trade. The problem is simply stated. We can produce food and other goods and services in abundance in Canada. There is no material reason why a single Canadian should go hungry or homeless or unclad because of the condition of world trade. We must, no matter how it may shock our conservative mentalities, set about finding a third method of building prosperity in Canada. We must devise and proceed to put into operation a system of distribution amongst our own people which will permit them to enjoy the full fruits that will flow from total use of all our resources.
In brief, that is exactly what Social Credit says is the solution.
Mr. Speaker, I desire to move, seconded by Mr. Ralston, that the house shall meet at four o'clock to-morrow afternoon.

Motion agreed to.
It being ten minutes past eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, June 30, 1944
